It is firmly established in Muslim and the authors of the Sunan, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) "used to recite in the Fajr prayer on Friday, *Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* (surah al-Sajdah) and *Hal Ata 'ala al-insan* (surah al-Insan) [al-Dahr: 1]."

It was also recorded by al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others from the same narrator.

Abu 'Ubayd in *Fada'il*, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Jabir, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would not sleep until he recited *Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* (the surah of al-Sajdah) and *Tabaraka alladhi bi-yadihi al-mulk* (surah al-Mulk) [al-Mulk: 1]."

Abu Nasr, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, traced back to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever prays four rak'ahs after the final 'Isha' prayer, reciting in the first two *Qul ya ayyuha al-kafirun* [al-Kafirun: 1] and *Qul huwa Allahu ahad* [al-Ikhlas: 1], and in the last two *Tabaraka alladhi bi-yadihi al-mulk* [al-Mulk: 1] and *Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* [al-Sajdah: 1], will have them recorded for him as equal to four rak'ahs on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr)."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ibn 'Umar that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites *Tabaraka alladhi bi-yadihi al-mulk* [al-Mulk: 1] and *Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* (surah al-Sajdah) between Maghrib and the final 'Isha' prayer, it is as if he stood (in prayer) on the Night of Power."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from 'A'ishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites in one night *Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* (surah al-Sajdah), *Ya Sin*, *Iqtarabat al-sa'ah* [al-Qamar: 1], and *Tabaraka alladhi bi-yadihi al-mulk*, they will be for him a light and a protection from Satan, and an elevation in ranks until the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn al-Durays recorded from al-Musayyib ibn Rafi' that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "*Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* will come on the Day of Resurrection with two wings, shading its companion and saying: 'There is no path against him, there is no path against him.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: *Alif Lam Mim*. We have already discussed the opening of this surah and its grammatical position (i'rab, grammatical analysis) in surah al-Baqarah, and in many places concerning the openings of the surahs.

The nominative case of *Tanzil* is either as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a predicate following a predicate, on the assumption that *Alif Lam Mim* is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as the predicate of *Alif Lam Mim*, on the assumption that it is the name of the surah. *La rayba fihi* is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). It is also permissible that *Tanzil* is nominative as the subject, with its predicate being *la rayba fihi*, and *min Rabb al-'alamin* in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. It is also permissible that all of these are predicates of the omitted subject before *Tanzil*, or of *Alif Lam Mim* on the assumption that it is a subject, not on the assumption that it is a series of letters listed in the manner of enumeration.

Makki said: The best of these readings is that *la rayba fihi* is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and *min Rabb al-'alamin* is the predicate. The meaning according to these readings is: the revelation of the Book being recited is beyond doubt and uncertainty, and it is sent down from the Lord of the worlds, and it is not a lie, nor sorcery, nor soothsaying, nor "the myths of the ancients."

The *am* in ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ is the disjunctive *am* meaning "rather," together with the interrogative hamzah, that is: "Rather, do they say he has fabricated it?" It shifts away from the earlier statement to what the disbelievers believe, with a question that carries rebuke and reproach. The meaning of *iftarahu* is that he made it up and fabricated it.

Then He turns away from their belief to explain what is the truth concerning the Book, and says: ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾. Thus He, glorified is He, refuted them in their claim of fabrication. Then He explained the reason for which the revelation was sent down, saying: ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you﴾. These are the Arabs, who were an unlettered nation to whom no messenger had come. It was also said: specifically the Quraysh. The second object of *tunzira* (to warn) is omitted, meaning: that you may warn a people of the punishment. The clause ﴿to whom no warner has come﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and *min qablika* is an adjective of *nadhir* (warner).

Abu Hayyan allowed that *ma* could be a relative pronoun, the sense being: "that you may warn a people of the punishment which a warner from before you had brought to them." This is very weak, because the intended meaning is the causation of the sending down by warning to a people to whom no warner had come before him, not the causation of it by warning to a people who had already been warned with what he warned them of. It was also said: the intended people are the people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah), the period between 'Isa and Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿So that they may be guided﴾ means in hope that they will be guided, or in order that they may be guided.

﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days; then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾. The explanation of this verse has already been given in surah al-A'raf. Its purpose here is to make them know the perfection of His power and the greatness of His creation, so that they may hear the Qur'an and reflect upon it. The meaning of *khalaqa* is: brought into existence and originated.

Al-Hasan said: the days here are days of this world. It was said: the duration of a day is a thousand years of worldly years, as said by al-Dahhak.

Accordingly, the days here are days of the Hereafter, not days of this world. And *thumma* in ﴿then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ is not for sequence. The explanation of this has been given fully.

﴿He has no guardian or intercessor besides Him﴾: that is, you have no guardian besides Allah, or besides His punishment, who would support you and turn back His punishment from you, nor any intercessor who would intercede for you with Him. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ Remembering here means reflecting and contemplating, and hearing these admonitions as one who understands and reasons, so that you may benefit from them.

﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾. When He, glorified is He, had explained the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, He explained His management of their affairs: that is, He firmly establishes the affair by His decree and measure, from the heaven to the earth. The meaning is: He sends down His command from the highest of the heavens to the farthest depths of the seventh earth, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth their like; the command descends among them﴾ [al-Talaq: 12]. The distance between the lowest heaven and the earth beneath it, in descent and ascent, is a thousand years of worldly days.

It was also said: the intended affairs are the commands concerning deeds; that is, He sends it down arranged from the heaven to the earth.

It was also said: He arranges the affairs of this world through heavenly causes, including the angels and others, whose rulings and effects descend to the earth.

It was also said: the revelation descends with Jibril.

It was also said: the Throne is the place of management, just as what is beneath the Throne is the place of detailing, as in His saying: ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ﴿He arranges the affair, detailing the signs﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2], and what is beneath the heavens is the place of disposal.

Allah said: ﴿And We have certainly diversified it among them that they may remember﴾ [al-Furqan: 50]. Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned the management of the affair, He said: ﴿Then it ascends to Him in a day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count﴾. That is: then that affair returns, and that management goes back to Him, glorified is He, in a day whose measure is a thousand years of worldly days. This is according to the distance of descent from the heaven and ascent from the earth, as we have mentioned.

It was also said: the meaning is that it ascends to Him on the Day of Resurrection, whose measure is a thousand years of worldly days, and that is when the affair of this world ends and whoever is in it dies.

It was also said: it is the reports of the people of the earth, which ascend to Him with the angels whom He sends to them. The meaning is that He establishes that with Him and records in the scrolls of His angels what the people of the earth did at every time, until the period of this world reaches its end.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿it ascends to Him﴾ is that it becomes established in His knowledge as existing in actuality, in a period of time whose measure is a thousand years, and the intended meaning is the long extent of time between the management of events and their occurrence.

It was also said: He arranges the affair of daily events by establishing them in the Preserved Tablet, and the angels then descend with them, and then they ascend to Him in a time that is like a thousand years of worldly days.

It was also said: He decrees a decree of a thousand years, and the angels descend with it, and then they ascend after the thousand for another thousand.

It was also said: the intended meaning is that the deeds which are acts of obedience are arranged by Allah, glorified is He, and His angels descend with them; then only the sincere among them ascend to Him after a long period, because of the scarcity of the sincere among His servants.

It was also said: the pronoun in *ya'ruju* refers to the deeds; the meaning is that the deeds ascend to Him after a long period, because of the scarcity of the sincere among His servants.

It was also said: the pronoun in *ya'ruju* refers to the King, even though he has not been mentioned, because it is understood from the context. It has come explicitly in His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. The pronoun in *ilayhi* refers to the heaven according to the usage of one who mentions it, or to the place of the King to which he returns, which is where Allah has settled him.

It was also said: the meaning is: He arranges the affair of the sun in its rising, its setting, and its return to its place of rising, in a day whose distance is a thousand years. It was also said: the meaning is that the King ascends to Allah in a day whose measure, if someone other than the King traveled it, would be a thousand years, because the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years. So the distance of descent from the heaven to the earth and of return from the earth to the heaven is a thousand years. Several exegetes preferred this view, among them Ibn Jarir.

It was also said: the distance of descent is a thousand years, and the distance of ascent is a thousand years, narrated from al-Dahhak.

This "day" is an expression for a period measured as a thousand years, and it is not intended to mean the named day, which is the duration of daylight between two nights. The Arabs do sometimes express a period by "day," as the poet said:

*Two days: a day of standing-places and of assemblies, and a day of marching against the enemies, a discipline.*

The poet did not mean two specific days; rather he meant that their time is divided into two halves, and he expressed each of the two halves by a day.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read *ya'ruju* in the active voice.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read it in the passive voice, the original being *yu'raju bihi* (it is ascended with it), and then the preposition was removed so the pronoun became implicit.

A group of scholars raised a difficulty in reconciling this verse with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4].

It was said in reply: the Day of Resurrection has a measure of a thousand years of worldly days, but because of its difficulty and the severity of its terrors for the disbelievers, it is like fifty thousand years. The Arabs often describe a day of hardship as long, just as they describe a day of happiness as short, as the poet said:

*And a day, like the shadow of a spear, its length was shortened by the blood of the wineskin for us and the lining up of the lutes.*

And another's saying:

*And a day, like the thumb of a cat, I cut it short.*

It was also said: the Day of Resurrection has days in it, some of which measure a thousand years and some of which measure fifty thousand years.

It was also said: these are different times in which the disbeliever is punished with one kind of punishment for a thousand years, then he is moved to another kind, and he is punished with it for fifty thousand years.

It was also said: the stations of the Resurrection are fifty stations, each station being a thousand years. So the meaning of ﴿it ascends to Him in a day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ is that it ascends to Him at one of those times, or at one of those stations.

Al-Tha'labi related from Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak that by His words ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4], God meant the distance from the earth to Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary), which is the station of Jibril. The meaning is that Jibril and the angels with him travel in that station to the earth a distance of fifty thousand years within the span of one day of the days of this world. By His words ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ He meant the distance between the earth and the lowest heaven, descending and ascending, which is a measure of a thousand years of the days of this world.

It has also been said that this refers to the extent of the carrying out of the command, because one whose command is carried out to the utmost extent in one day or two days, and then ends, is not like one whose command is carried out over lengthy years. So His words ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ mean that He manages the affair in a time in which one day is a thousand years. How much, then, is a month in it, and how much is a year in it? On this view there is no difference between a thousand years and fifty thousand years. It has also been said other than this.

The scholar of the Ummah, Ibn 'Abbas, paused when he was asked about the two verses, as will come later in the discussion, God willing.

The majority of readers recited ﴿مِمَّا تَعُدُّونَ﴾ ("of what you count") with the second-person form (taʿuddūn, "you count"). Al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Ibn Waththab and al-A'mash recited it with the third-person form (yaʿuddūn, "they count").

The demonstrative in His words ﴿That﴾ refers to God, glorified is He, in respect of His being described by those attributes. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, that is, the One who knows what is hidden from creation and what is present to them.

In this there is an implication of warning, because when He, glorified is He, knows what is absent and what is present, He will recompense every doer for his deed.

Or, He manages the affair as His wisdom requires; ﴿the Mighty, the Subduer, the Merciful toward His servants﴾. These are predicates of that subject.

Likewise His words ﴿who perfected everything He created﴾ are another predicate.

The majority recited ﴿khalaqahu﴾ with a fatha on the lam (khalaqahu, a past-tense verb). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited it with the lam sukun (khalqahu, a verbal noun).

On the first reading, it is a past-tense verb serving as a qualifier (na't) of a thing, so it is in the genitive position (mahall jarr).

Abu 'Ubaydah and Abu Hatim preferred the reading of the majority. It may also be that it is a qualifier of the antecedent (al-mudaf), so it is in the accusative position (mahall nasb).

On the second reading, its accusative case has several possibilities. The first is that it is a substitute for "kulla shay'" (everything) by way of badal ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), with the pronoun referring to "kulla shay'". This is the well-known view among the grammarians.

The second is that it is badal kull min kull (substitution of the whole by the whole), with the pronoun referring to God, glorified is He. The meaning of ahsana is hassana (made beautiful), because there is nothing that is not created in the way that wisdom requires, so all created things are beautiful.

The third is that kulla shay' is the first object (maf'ul awwal), and khalqahu is the second object (maf'ul thani), by way of tadmin (implying one verb's meaning within another) of ahsana with the meaning of a'ta (gave). The meaning is: He gave everything the creation that He specifically assigned to it.

It has also been said that it implies the meaning of alhama (inspired). Al-Farra' said: He inspired His creatures with everything they need.

The fourth is that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) emphasizing the content of the sentence, that is: He created it with a creation, like His words ﴿the handiwork of God﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. This is the view of Sibawayh, and the pronoun refers to God, glorified is He.

The fifth is that it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid), and the meaning is: He made beautiful everything in its creation. The meaning of the verse is that He perfected and made firm the creation of His creatures. Some creatures, though not beautiful in themselves, are perfected and firm, so this verse has a meaning like the meaning of ﴿He gave everything its creation﴾, that is, He did not create man in the form of the beast, nor the beast in the form of man. It has also been said that it is general in wording and specific in meaning: that is, He made beautiful the creation of every beautiful thing.

﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾, meaning Adam, whom He created from clay, so he became in a wondrous form and a beautiful shape.

﴿Then He made his descendants﴾, that is, his offspring, ﴿from an extract﴾. Offspring were called sulalah because they are drawn out (tusall) from the origin and separated from it. Its explanation has already been given in Surat al-Mu'minun. The meaning of ﴿from a despised water﴾ is from a water that is degraded, of no consequence in people's eyes, and it is semen.

Al-Zajjaj said: from a weak water.

﴿Then He proportioned him﴾, that is, the man whose creation He began from clay, namely Adam, or the whole species. The meaning is that He balanced his creation, shaped his form, and harmonized his limbs. ﴿And breathed into him of His Spirit﴾. The idafah (attribution) is for honor and dignity. This attribution strengthens the view that the discussion concerns Adam and not his descendants, although it is possible to direct it to all of them.

Then He addressed the whole species, saying ﴿And He made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾, that is, He created these things for you, completing His blessing upon you and perfecting His proportioning of your creation, so that blessings gather for you: you hear everything that can be heard, you see everything that can be seen, you understand everything that can be understood, and you comprehend everything that can be comprehended. He used the singular "hearing" (al-sam') because it is a verbal noun (masdar) that covers the few and the many. He singled out hearing by mentioning it as a verbal noun, not sight and heart, which He mentioned by their names, and for this reason they are in the plural. This is because hearing is one power with one locus, which is the ear, and it has no choice in it, since sound reaches it and it cannot repel it, nor can it specify hearing for some heard things over others. Sight, by contrast, has the eye as its locus, and it has choice in it, since it moves toward the seen object and not others, and it closes its eyelids when it does not wish to see something. Likewise the heart has a kind of choice in its perception, so it comprehends this and not that, and it understands this and not that.

Readers recited ﴿wa-bada'a﴾ with hamzah (the majority). Al-Zuhri recited it with a pure alif, without hamzah. The accusative of ﴿little are the thanks you give﴾ is either a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a little thanks," or a qualifier of an omitted time, meaning "a little time."

In this there is an explanation of their disbelief in God's blessings and their abandonment of giving thanks for them, except in rare circumstances.

﴿And they say: "When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ The readers' difference over this hamzah and the hamzah after it has already been mentioned. Dalal (going astray) means being hidden. It is said: the dead one strayed in the dust when he became hidden and lost. The Arabs say of a thing that another thing has overcome until its trace is hidden: it has strayed (dalla). From this is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"I was a speck of dust in a murky, foaming wave,
Which the flood cast about, and it strayed in a straying."

Qutrub said: the meaning of "we have gone astray in the earth" is: we have become absent in the earth.

The majority recited ﴿dalalna﴾ with a dad with a fatha and a lam with a fatha, meaning we went away, we became dust, and we became absent from eyes. Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Raja' recited ﴿dalilna﴾ with a kasrah on the lam, which is the dialect of the upper region of Najd. Al-Jawhari said: the people of the upper region say dalilt with the kasrah.

He said: and aḍallahu means he lost it and destroyed it. It is said: the dead one strayed when he was buried.

Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, al-A'mash and Aban ibn Sa'id recited ﴿salalna﴾ with an unpointed sad and a lam with a fatha, meaning we stank.

Al-Nahhas said: "salalna" is not known in the language, but it is said: the meat stank (salla al-lahm) when it became rotten.

Al-Jawhari said: the meat stinks (yasill) with a kasrah, sululan, when it becomes rotten, whether cooked or raw. From this is the saying of al-Hutay'ah:

"That is a youth who gives generously with his ability,
The stench does not spoil the meat near him."

﴿Shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, that is, shall we be raised and become living? The interrogation is one of denial.

This is the saying of the disbelieving deniers of the resurrection. So God, glorified is He, turned from explaining their disbelief in denying the resurrection to explaining something more emphatic, which is their disbelief in meeting God. So He said ﴿Rather, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾, that is, they deny Him out of arrogance and obstinacy, for their acknowledgment that He is the originator of creation necessitates their acknowledgment that He is capable of restoring it.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to make the truth clear to them and to refute the falsehood they claimed, so He said ﴿Say: "The angel of death who has been charged with you will take you; then to your Lord you will be returned."﴾ It is said: God caused him to die (tawaffahu Allah) and took his soul fully (istawfa ruhahu) when He took it to Himself. The angel of death is 'Izra'il. The meaning of "charged with you" is: charged with taking your souls when your appointed terms arrive. ﴿Then to your Lord you will be returned﴾, that is, you will go back to Him alive through resurrection and rising, and not to anyone else, and He will recompense you for your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿He manages the affair﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: this is in the world; the angels ascend in a Day whose measure is a thousand years.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from him concerning His words ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years﴾, that he said: it is one of the six days in which God created the heavens and the earth.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Mulaykah, who said: I entered upon 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, I and 'Abd Allah ibn Fayruz, the freedman of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. Ibn Fayruz said to him: O Abu 'Abbas, His words ﴿He manages the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day whose measure is a thousand years﴾. Ibn 'Abbas seemed to suspect him, so he said: what is a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years? He said: I only asked you so that you would inform me. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are two days which God mentioned in His Book; God knows best about them, and I dislike saying in the Book of God what I do not know. Time passed through its blows until I sat with Ibn al-Musayyab, and a man asked him about them, but he did not inform him and did not know.

So I said: Shall I not inform you of what I witnessed from Ibn 'Abbas? He said: Yes. So I informed him, and he said to the questioner: This is Ibn 'Abbas, who refused to say anything about them, and he is more knowledgeable than I am.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿whose measure is a thousand years﴾ that he said: The middle of the day does not come, in a Day that is the measure of one of the days of the world, until He judges among the servants, so that the people of Paradise descend into Paradise and the people of the Fire into the Fire. And if it were to another, it would not finish in fifty thousand years.

Ibn Jarir also related from him, concerning His words ﴿then it ascends to Him in a Day﴾, that it is one of your days, and the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to recite ﴿Who perfected everything He created﴾ and said: I have not seen that monkeys are beautiful, but He perfected their creation.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, concerning the verse, that he said: As for the buttocks of monkeys, they are not beautiful, but He perfected their creation. He said: khalaqahu means its form. He said: ﴿ahsana kulla shay'﴾ includes the ugly and the beautiful, and scorpions and snakes, and everything He created; and no one other than Him perfects anything of that.

Al-Tabarani related from Abu Umamah, who said: "While we were with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, we met 'Amr ibn Zurarah al-Ansari in a garment that he had let hang down. The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, took hold of the edge of his garment and said: 'O Messenger of God, I have thin calves.' The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'O 'Amr ibn Zurarah, God, Mighty and Majestic, has made beautiful everything He created. O 'Amr ibn Zurarah, God does not love those who let their garments hang down.'"

Ahmad and al-Tabarani related from al-Sharid ibn Suwayd, who said: "The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, saw a man who had let his izar hang down, and he said: 'Raise your izar.' The man said: 'O Messenger of God, I am knock-kneed, my knees knock together.' He said: 'Raise your izar; every creation of God is beautiful.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 32, verses 2–11 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan, as narrated by Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il*, from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Ibn al-Najjar recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "It is Meccan except for three verses, from ﴿Is one who was a believer﴾ to the end of the three verses [al-Sajdah: 18–20]." Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said the same. It was also said: "Except for five verses, from His words ﴿Whose sides forsake their beds﴾ to His words ﴿that which you used to deny﴾ [al-Sajdah: 16–20]."

It is firmly established in Muslim and the authors of the Sunan, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) "used to recite in the Fajr prayer on Friday, *Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* (surah al-Sajdah) and *Hal Ata 'ala al-insan* (surah al-Insan) [al-Dahr: 1]."

It was also recorded by al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others from the same narrator.

Abu 'Ubayd in *Fada'il*, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Jabir, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would not sleep until he recited *Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* (the surah of al-Sajdah) and *Tabaraka alladhi bi-yadihi al-mulk* (surah al-Mulk) [al-Mulk: 1]."

Abu Nasr, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, traced back to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever prays four rak'ahs after the final 'Isha' prayer, reciting in the first two *Qul ya ayyuha al-kafirun* [al-Kafirun: 1] and *Qul huwa Allahu ahad* [al-Ikhlas: 1], and in the last two *Tabaraka alladhi bi-yadihi al-mulk* [al-Mulk: 1] and *Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* [al-Sajdah: 1], will have them recorded for him as equal to four rak'ahs on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr)."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ibn 'Umar that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites *Tabaraka alladhi bi-yadihi al-mulk* [al-Mulk: 1] and *Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* (surah al-Sajdah) between Maghrib and the final 'Isha' prayer, it is as if he stood (in prayer) on the Night of Power."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from 'A'ishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites in one night *Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* (surah al-Sajdah), *Ya Sin*, *Iqtarabat al-sa'ah* [al-Qamar: 1], and *Tabaraka alladhi bi-yadihi al-mulk*, they will be for him a light and a protection from Satan, and an elevation in ranks until the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn al-Durays recorded from al-Musayyib ibn Rafi' that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "*Alif Lam Mim Tanzil* will come on the Day of Resurrection with two wings, shading its companion and saying: 'There is no path against him, there is no path against him.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: *Alif Lam Mim*. We have already discussed the opening of this surah and its grammatical position (i'rab, grammatical analysis) in surah al-Baqarah, and in many places concerning the openings of the surahs.

The nominative case of *Tanzil* is either as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a predicate following a predicate, on the assumption that *Alif Lam Mim* is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as the predicate of *Alif Lam Mim*, on the assumption that it is the name of the surah. *La rayba fihi* is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). It is also permissible that *Tanzil* is nominative as the subject, with its predicate being *la rayba fihi*, and *min Rabb al-'alamin* in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. It is also permissible that all of these are predicates of the omitted subject before *Tanzil*, or of *Alif Lam Mim* on the assumption that it is a subject, not on the assumption that it is a series of letters listed in the manner of enumeration.

Makki said: The best of these readings is that *la rayba fihi* is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and *min Rabb al-'alamin* is the predicate. The meaning according to these readings is: the revelation of the Book being recited is beyond doubt and uncertainty, and it is sent down from the Lord of the worlds, and it is not a lie, nor sorcery, nor soothsaying, nor "the myths of the ancients."

The *am* in ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ is the disjunctive *am* meaning "rather," together with the interrogative hamzah, that is: "Rather, do they say he has fabricated it?" It shifts away from the earlier statement to what the disbelievers believe, with a question that carries rebuke and reproach. The meaning of *iftarahu* is that he made it up and fabricated it.

Then He turns away from their belief to explain what is the truth concerning the Book, and says: ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾. Thus He, glorified is He, refuted them in their claim of fabrication. Then He explained the reason for which the revelation was sent down, saying: ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you﴾. These are the Arabs, who were an unlettered nation to whom no messenger had come. It was also said: specifically the Quraysh. The second object of *tunzira* (to warn) is omitted, meaning: that you may warn a people of the punishment. The clause ﴿to whom no warner has come﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and *min qablika* is an adjective of *nadhir* (warner).

Abu Hayyan allowed that *ma* could be a relative pronoun, the sense being: "that you may warn a people of the punishment which a warner from before you had brought to them." This is very weak, because the intended meaning is the causation of the sending down by warning to a people to whom no warner had come before him, not the causation of it by warning to a people who had already been warned with what he warned them of. It was also said: the intended people are the people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah), the period between 'Isa and Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿So that they may be guided﴾ means in hope that they will be guided, or in order that they may be guided.

﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days; then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾. The explanation of this verse has already been given in surah al-A'raf. Its purpose here is to make them know the perfection of His power and the greatness of His creation, so that they may hear the Qur'an and reflect upon it. The meaning of *khalaqa* is: brought into existence and originated.

Al-Hasan said: the days here are days of this world. It was said: the duration of a day is a thousand years of worldly years, as said by al-Dahhak.

Accordingly, the days here are days of the Hereafter, not days of this world. And *thumma* in ﴿then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ is not for sequence. The explanation of this has been given fully.

﴿He has no guardian or intercessor besides Him﴾: that is, you have no guardian besides Allah, or besides His punishment, who would support you and turn back His punishment from you, nor any intercessor who would intercede for you with Him. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ Remembering here means reflecting and contemplating, and hearing these admonitions as one who understands and reasons, so that you may benefit from them.

﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾. When He, glorified is He, had explained the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, He explained His management of their affairs: that is, He firmly establishes the affair by His decree and measure, from the heaven to the earth. The meaning is: He sends down His command from the highest of the heavens to the farthest depths of the seventh earth, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth their like; the command descends among them﴾ [al-Talaq: 12]. The distance between the lowest heaven and the earth beneath it, in descent and ascent, is a thousand years of worldly days.

It was also said: the intended affairs are the commands concerning deeds; that is, He sends it down arranged from the heaven to the earth.

It was also said: He arranges the affairs of this world through heavenly causes, including the angels and others, whose rulings and effects descend to the earth.

It was also said: the revelation descends with Jibril.

It was also said: the Throne is the place of management, just as what is beneath the Throne is the place of detailing, as in His saying: ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ﴿He arranges the affair, detailing the signs﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2], and what is beneath the heavens is the place of disposal.

Allah said: ﴿And We have certainly diversified it among them that they may remember﴾ [al-Furqan: 50]. Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned the management of the affair, He said: ﴿Then it ascends to Him in a day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count﴾. That is: then that affair returns, and that management goes back to Him, glorified is He, in a day whose measure is a thousand years of worldly days. This is according to the distance of descent from the heaven and ascent from the earth, as we have mentioned.

It was also said: the meaning is that it ascends to Him on the Day of Resurrection, whose measure is a thousand years of worldly days, and that is when the affair of this world ends and whoever is in it dies.

It was also said: it is the reports of the people of the earth, which ascend to Him with the angels whom He sends to them. The meaning is that He establishes that with Him and records in the scrolls of His angels what the people of the earth did at every time, until the period of this world reaches its end.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿it ascends to Him﴾ is that it becomes established in His knowledge as existing in actuality, in a period of time whose measure is a thousand years, and the intended meaning is the long extent of time between the management of events and their occurrence.

It was also said: He arranges the affair of daily events by establishing them in the Preserved Tablet, and the angels then descend with them, and then they ascend to Him in a time that is like a thousand years of worldly days.

It was also said: He decrees a decree of a thousand years, and the angels descend with it, and then they ascend after the thousand for another thousand.

It was also said: the intended meaning is that the deeds which are acts of obedience are arranged by Allah, glorified is He, and His angels descend with them; then only the sincere among them ascend to Him after a long period, because of the scarcity of the sincere among His servants.

It was also said: the pronoun in *ya'ruju* refers to the deeds; the meaning is that the deeds ascend to Him after a long period, because of the scarcity of the sincere among His servants.

It was also said: the pronoun in *ya'ruju* refers to the King, even though he has not been mentioned, because it is understood from the context. It has come explicitly in His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. The pronoun in *ilayhi* refers to the heaven according to the usage of one who mentions it, or to the place of the King to which he returns, which is where Allah has settled him.

It was also said: the meaning is: He arranges the affair of the sun in its rising, its setting, and its return to its place of rising, in a day whose distance is a thousand years. It was also said: the meaning is that the King ascends to Allah in a day whose measure, if someone other than the King traveled it, would be a thousand years, because the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years. So the distance of descent from the heaven to the earth and of return from the earth to the heaven is a thousand years. Several exegetes preferred this view, among them Ibn Jarir.

It was also said: the distance of descent is a thousand years, and the distance of ascent is a thousand years, narrated from al-Dahhak.

This "day" is an expression for a period measured as a thousand years, and it is not intended to mean the named day, which is the duration of daylight between two nights. The Arabs do sometimes express a period by "day," as the poet said:

*Two days: a day of standing-places and of assemblies, and a day of marching against the enemies, a discipline.*

The poet did not mean two specific days; rather he meant that their time is divided into two halves, and he expressed each of the two halves by a day.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read *ya'ruju* in the active voice.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read it in the passive voice, the original being *yu'raju bihi* (it is ascended with it), and then the preposition was removed so the pronoun became implicit.

A group of scholars raised a difficulty in reconciling this verse with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4].

It was said in reply: the Day of Resurrection has a measure of a thousand years of worldly days, but because of its difficulty and the severity of its terrors for the disbelievers, it is like fifty thousand years. The Arabs often describe a day of hardship as long, just as they describe a day of happiness as short, as the poet said:

*And a day, like the shadow of a spear, its length was shortened by the blood of the wineskin for us and the lining up of the lutes.*

And another's saying:

*And a day, like the thumb of a cat, I cut it short.*

It was also said: the Day of Resurrection has days in it, some of which measure a thousand years and some of which measure fifty thousand years.

It was also said: these are different times in which the disbeliever is punished with one kind of punishment for a thousand years, then he is moved to another kind, and he is punished with it for fifty thousand years.

It was also said: the stations of the Resurrection are fifty stations, each station being a thousand years. So the meaning of ﴿it ascends to Him in a day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ is that it ascends to Him at one of those times, or at one of those stations.

Al-Tha'labi related from Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak that by His words ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4], God meant the distance from the earth to Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary), which is the station of Jibril. The meaning is that Jibril and the angels with him travel in that station to the earth a distance of fifty thousand years within the span of one day of the days of this world. By His words ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ He meant the distance between the earth and the lowest heaven, descending and ascending, which is a measure of a thousand years of the days of this world.

It has also been said that this refers to the extent of the carrying out of the command, because one whose command is carried out to the utmost extent in one day or two days, and then ends, is not like one whose command is carried out over lengthy years. So His words ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ mean that He manages the affair in a time in which one day is a thousand years. How much, then, is a month in it, and how much is a year in it? On this view there is no difference between a thousand years and fifty thousand years. It has also been said other than this.

The scholar of the Ummah, Ibn 'Abbas, paused when he was asked about the two verses, as will come later in the discussion, God willing.

The majority of readers recited ﴿مِمَّا تَعُدُّونَ﴾ ("of what you count") with the second-person form (taʿuddūn, "you count"). Al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Ibn Waththab and al-A'mash recited it with the third-person form (yaʿuddūn, "they count").

The demonstrative in His words ﴿That﴾ refers to God, glorified is He, in respect of His being described by those attributes. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, that is, the One who knows what is hidden from creation and what is present to them.

In this there is an implication of warning, because when He, glorified is He, knows what is absent and what is present, He will recompense every doer for his deed.

Or, He manages the affair as His wisdom requires; ﴿the Mighty, the Subduer, the Merciful toward His servants﴾. These are predicates of that subject.

Likewise His words ﴿who perfected everything He created﴾ are another predicate.

The majority recited ﴿khalaqahu﴾ with a fatha on the lam (khalaqahu, a past-tense verb). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited it with the lam sukun (khalqahu, a verbal noun).

On the first reading, it is a past-tense verb serving as a qualifier (na't) of a thing, so it is in the genitive position (mahall jarr).

Abu 'Ubaydah and Abu Hatim preferred the reading of the majority. It may also be that it is a qualifier of the antecedent (al-mudaf), so it is in the accusative position (mahall nasb).

On the second reading, its accusative case has several possibilities. The first is that it is a substitute for "kulla shay'" (everything) by way of badal ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), with the pronoun referring to "kulla shay'". This is the well-known view among the grammarians.

The second is that it is badal kull min kull (substitution of the whole by the whole), with the pronoun referring to God, glorified is He. The meaning of ahsana is hassana (made beautiful), because there is nothing that is not created in the way that wisdom requires, so all created things are beautiful.

The third is that kulla shay' is the first object (maf'ul awwal), and khalqahu is the second object (maf'ul thani), by way of tadmin (implying one verb's meaning within another) of ahsana with the meaning of a'ta (gave). The meaning is: He gave everything the creation that He specifically assigned to it.

It has also been said that it implies the meaning of alhama (inspired). Al-Farra' said: He inspired His creatures with everything they need.

The fourth is that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) emphasizing the content of the sentence, that is: He created it with a creation, like His words ﴿the handiwork of God﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. This is the view of Sibawayh, and the pronoun refers to God, glorified is He.

The fifth is that it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid), and the meaning is: He made beautiful everything in its creation. The meaning of the verse is that He perfected and made firm the creation of His creatures. Some creatures, though not beautiful in themselves, are perfected and firm, so this verse has a meaning like the meaning of ﴿He gave everything its creation﴾, that is, He did not create man in the form of the beast, nor the beast in the form of man. It has also been said that it is general in wording and specific in meaning: that is, He made beautiful the creation of every beautiful thing.

﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾, meaning Adam, whom He created from clay, so he became in a wondrous form and a beautiful shape.

﴿Then He made his descendants﴾, that is, his offspring, ﴿from an extract﴾. Offspring were called sulalah because they are drawn out (tusall) from the origin and separated from it. Its explanation has already been given in Surat al-Mu'minun. The meaning of ﴿from a despised water﴾ is from a water that is degraded, of no consequence in people's eyes, and it is semen.

Al-Zajjaj said: from a weak water.

﴿Then He proportioned him﴾, that is, the man whose creation He began from clay, namely Adam, or the whole species. The meaning is that He balanced his creation, shaped his form, and harmonized his limbs. ﴿And breathed into him of His Spirit﴾. The idafah (attribution) is for honor and dignity. This attribution strengthens the view that the discussion concerns Adam and not his descendants, although it is possible to direct it to all of them.

Then He addressed the whole species, saying ﴿And He made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾, that is, He created these things for you, completing His blessing upon you and perfecting His proportioning of your creation, so that blessings gather for you: you hear everything that can be heard, you see everything that can be seen, you understand everything that can be understood, and you comprehend everything that can be comprehended. He used the singular "hearing" (al-sam') because it is a verbal noun (masdar) that covers the few and the many. He singled out hearing by mentioning it as a verbal noun, not sight and heart, which He mentioned by their names, and for this reason they are in the plural. This is because hearing is one power with one locus, which is the ear, and it has no choice in it, since sound reaches it and it cannot repel it, nor can it specify hearing for some heard things over others. Sight, by contrast, has the eye as its locus, and it has choice in it, since it moves toward the seen object and not others, and it closes its eyelids when it does not wish to see something. Likewise the heart has a kind of choice in its perception, so it comprehends this and not that, and it understands this and not that.

Readers recited ﴿wa-bada'a﴾ with hamzah (the majority). Al-Zuhri recited it with a pure alif, without hamzah. The accusative of ﴿little are the thanks you give﴾ is either a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a little thanks," or a qualifier of an omitted time, meaning "a little time."

In this there is an explanation of their disbelief in God's blessings and their abandonment of giving thanks for them, except in rare circumstances.

﴿And they say: "When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ The readers' difference over this hamzah and the hamzah after it has already been mentioned. Dalal (going astray) means being hidden. It is said: the dead one strayed in the dust when he became hidden and lost. The Arabs say of a thing that another thing has overcome until its trace is hidden: it has strayed (dalla). From this is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"I was a speck of dust in a murky, foaming wave,
Which the flood cast about, and it strayed in a straying."

Qutrub said: the meaning of "we have gone astray in the earth" is: we have become absent in the earth.

The majority recited ﴿dalalna﴾ with a dad with a fatha and a lam with a fatha, meaning we went away, we became dust, and we became absent from eyes. Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Raja' recited ﴿dalilna﴾ with a kasrah on the lam, which is the dialect of the upper region of Najd. Al-Jawhari said: the people of the upper region say dalilt with the kasrah.

He said: and aḍallahu means he lost it and destroyed it. It is said: the dead one strayed when he was buried.

Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, al-A'mash and Aban ibn Sa'id recited ﴿salalna﴾ with an unpointed sad and a lam with a fatha, meaning we stank.

Al-Nahhas said: "salalna" is not known in the language, but it is said: the meat stank (salla al-lahm) when it became rotten.

Al-Jawhari said: the meat stinks (yasill) with a kasrah, sululan, when it becomes rotten, whether cooked or raw. From this is the saying of al-Hutay'ah:

"That is a youth who gives generously with his ability,
The stench does not spoil the meat near him."

﴿Shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, that is, shall we be raised and become living? The interrogation is one of denial.

This is the saying of the disbelieving deniers of the resurrection. So God, glorified is He, turned from explaining their disbelief in denying the resurrection to explaining something more emphatic, which is their disbelief in meeting God. So He said ﴿Rather, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾, that is, they deny Him out of arrogance and obstinacy, for their acknowledgment that He is the originator of creation necessitates their acknowledgment that He is capable of restoring it.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to make the truth clear to them and to refute the falsehood they claimed, so He said ﴿Say: "The angel of death who has been charged with you will take you; then to your Lord you will be returned."﴾ It is said: God caused him to die (tawaffahu Allah) and took his soul fully (istawfa ruhahu) when He took it to Himself. The angel of death is 'Izra'il. The meaning of "charged with you" is: charged with taking your souls when your appointed terms arrive. ﴿Then to your Lord you will be returned﴾, that is, you will go back to Him alive through resurrection and rising, and not to anyone else, and He will recompense you for your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿He manages the affair﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: this is in the world; the angels ascend in a Day whose measure is a thousand years.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from him concerning His words ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years﴾, that he said: it is one of the six days in which God created the heavens and the earth.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Mulaykah, who said: I entered upon 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, I and 'Abd Allah ibn Fayruz, the freedman of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. Ibn Fayruz said to him: O Abu 'Abbas, His words ﴿He manages the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day whose measure is a thousand years﴾. Ibn 'Abbas seemed to suspect him, so he said: what is a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years? He said: I only asked you so that you would inform me. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are two days which God mentioned in His Book; God knows best about them, and I dislike saying in the Book of God what I do not know. Time passed through its blows until I sat with Ibn al-Musayyab, and a man asked him about them, but he did not inform him and did not know.

So I said: Shall I not inform you of what I witnessed from Ibn 'Abbas? He said: Yes. So I informed him, and he said to the questioner: This is Ibn 'Abbas, who refused to say anything about them, and he is more knowledgeable than I am.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿whose measure is a thousand years﴾ that he said: The middle of the day does not come, in a Day that is the measure of one of the days of the world, until He judges among the servants, so that the people of Paradise descend into Paradise and the people of the Fire into the Fire. And if it were to another, it would not finish in fifty thousand years.

Ibn Jarir also related from him, concerning His words ﴿then it ascends to Him in a Day﴾, that it is one of your days, and the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to recite ﴿Who perfected everything He created﴾ and said: I have not seen that monkeys are beautiful, but He perfected their creation.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, concerning the verse, that he said: As for the buttocks of monkeys, they are not beautiful, but He perfected their creation. He said: khalaqahu means its form. He said: ﴿ahsana kulla shay'﴾ includes the ugly and the beautiful, and scorpions and snakes, and everything He created; and no one other than Him perfects anything of that.

Al-Tabarani related from Abu Umamah, who said: "While we were with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, we met 'Amr ibn Zurarah al-Ansari in a garment that he had let hang down. The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, took hold of the edge of his garment and said: 'O Messenger of God, I have thin calves.' The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'O 'Amr ibn Zurarah, God, Mighty and Majestic, has made beautiful everything He created. O 'Amr ibn Zurarah, God does not love those who let their garments hang down.'"

Ahmad and al-Tabarani related from al-Sharid ibn Suwayd, who said: "The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, saw a man who had let his izar hang down, and he said: 'Raise your izar.' The man said: 'O Messenger of God, I am knock-kneed, my knees knock together.' He said: 'Raise your izar; every creation of God is beautiful.'"

[p. 1151] **His words: ﴿Had you but seen the guilty, bowing their heads before their Lord﴾.** The "guilty" here are those who said, "When we have gone astray, shall we indeed be [brought back] anew?" The address is to anyone fit to receive it, or to the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ)).

It is also possible that "the guilty" refers to every guilty person, with those who made that statement included first and foremost. The phrase ﴿bowing their heads﴾ means lowering them in shame and remorse for what they committed in the world of shirk (association of partners with Allah) and disobedience to Him. The phrase ﴿before their Lord﴾ means at the time of His reckoning of them.

Al-Zajjaj said: The address to the Prophet (ﷺ) is an address to his community. The meaning is: "Had you seen, O Muhammad, the deniers of the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment, you would have seen a wondrous sight, [as they say,] ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾." That is, they say: "Our Lord, we now see what we used to deny, and we hear what we used to reject." It has also been said: "We have seen the truth of Your threat, and we have heard the confirmation of Your messengers." Thus these people saw when sight no longer benefited them, and heard when hearing no longer benefited them. ﴿So send us back﴾ to the world, "and we will do righteous deeds as You commanded us." ﴿Indeed, we are certain﴾, that is, affirming. It has also been said: affirming what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. They describe themselves as certain now, hoping for what they request, namely their return to the world. But how could that be? The word of Allah has already come due against them, for ﴿even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden, and they are indeed liars﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿we are certain﴾ is that the doubts which used to beset them in the world have now departed, since they have seen and heard what they have seen and heard. It is also possible that the meaning of ﴿we have seen and heard﴾ is "we have become among those who hear and see," so that there is no need to supply an object. It is also permissible for ﴿righteous﴾ (ṣāliḥan) to be the object of ﴿we will do﴾, just as it may be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The answer to ﴿Had you but seen﴾ (law, "had") is omitted, meaning: "you would have seen a dreadful matter and a terrifying horror."

**﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾.** This is a rebuttal of them when they asked for a return. That is: had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, guiding all people, so that none of them would have disbelieved.

Al-Nahhas said: Regarding the meaning of this there are two views: one is that it refers to the world, and the other is that it refers to the Hereafter. That is: had We willed, We would have sent them back to the world. ﴿But the word from Me has come due: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together﴾. The clause ﴿had We willed﴾ is understood as a clause introduced by a verb of saying, coordinated with what was understood before ﴿We have seen﴾, meaning: "and We say, had We willed..." The meaning of ﴿but the word from Me has come due﴾ is: My decree has taken effect, My predestination has been carried out, and My word has preceded. ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together﴾: this is the word that was decreed by Allah, became binding upon His servants, and whose decree took effect. The implication of this word is that He does not give every soul its guidance. He has decreed this against them because He, glorified is He, knew that they were of the wretched, and that they were among those who choose misguidance over guidance.

The fā' (so) in His words, ﴿So taste [the punishment] for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾, marks the order of the command to taste following what came before it. The bā' (for) in ﴿for having forgotten﴾ indicates causation, and it implies that their punishment is not merely due to the preceding decree, but to that and this together.

Scholars differed about the forgetting mentioned here. Some said it is genuine forgetting, the kind by which remembrance departs. Others said it is abandonment. According to the first view, the meaning is that they did not work for that Day, so they were like those who forget it and do not remember it. According to the second, a noun must be supplied before ﴿meeting﴾: "taste the punishment of the meeting of this your Day because of your abandonment of what you were commanded." Al-Mubarrad preferred the second view and recited:

*As if it were a skewer of a drinker, one who forgot it at the moment of its drawing out (?)* [He made the poem's point that forgetting means abandoning.]

That is, they abandoned it. Al-Dahhak and Yahya ibn Salam also said that forgetting here means abandoning. Yahya ibn Salam said: The meaning is: For having abandoned belief in the Resurrection on this Day, We abandon you from good. Al-Suddi said the same. Mujahid said: We abandon you in the punishment.

Muqatil said: When they enter the Fire, the guardians will say to them, "Taste the punishment for having forgotten." Here the word "taste" is used metaphorically for experiencing. Tufayl said:

*So taste as we tasted on the day of the ambush,*
*From the rage in our livers and the reproach.*

His words: ﴿And taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do﴾ are a repetition for emphasis. That is: taste the lasting punishment that never ends, for what you used to do in the world of disbelief and sins.

Al-Razi said in his Tafsir (exegesis): the demonstrative in His words, ﴿for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾, may have three possible referents: it may refer to the meeting, to the Day, or to the punishment.

The clause ﴿Only those believe in Our signs﴾ is a new sentence that explains who deserves guidance to belief and who does not. The meaning is: only those who affirm Our signs and benefit from them are ﴿those who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration﴾, and not others who are reminded of them, that is, admonished by them, but do not remember or believe in them. The phrase ﴿fall down in prostration﴾ means fall on their faces, prostrating, glorifying Allah's signs and fearing His might and punishment. ﴿And glorify their Lord with praise﴾, that is, they declare Him free of all that is unbefitting Him, while joined with praise for His blessings, the greatest and most complete of which is guidance to belief. The meaning is that they say in their prostration: "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," or "Glory be to my Lord the Most High and praise be to Him."

Sufyan said: The meaning is "pray out of praise for your Lord." The clause ﴿and they are not arrogant﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while they are humbly submissive to Allah, abasing themselves to Him, and not arrogant toward Him.

**﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾**, that is, they rise and lift themselves up. It is said: *jafā al-shay' 'an al-shay'* and *tajāfā 'anhu* when a thing does not cling to another and is set aside from it. ﴿Beds﴾ is the plural of *maḍja'* (bed), the place where one lies down. Al-Zajjaj and al-Rummani said: *tajāfī* and *tajaffī* are toward the upward direction, and likewise in pardoning the one who errs in abuse or the like. ﴿Sides﴾ is the plural of *janb*. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: their sides are forsaking their beds. These are those who pray at night (*mutahajjidūn*), who rise from their bedding for prayer. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ata', and the majority. The prayer intended is the voluntary night prayer (*tanafful*, supererogatory worship) without specification.

Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: it is voluntary prayer between Maghrib and 'Isha'. It has also been said: it is the 'Isha' prayer alone, a report from al-Hasan and 'Ata'. Al-Dahhak said: it is the 'Isha' and Fajr prayers in congregation. It has also been said: they are those who rise for the remembrance of Allah, whether in prayer or otherwise.

**﴿They call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾.** This clause is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, relating to the pronoun in ﴿their sides﴾. So it is a circumstantial clause following another circumstantial clause. It is also possible that the first clause is a new sentence explaining one kind of their acts of obedience. The meaning is: their sides forsake their beds while they call upon their Lord, fearing His punishment and hoping for His mercy.

**﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾**, that is, from what We have provided them, or from their provision. This is the obligatory charity. It has also been said: it is voluntary charity. The better view is to take it in general. The accusative of *khawfan wa-ṭam'an* (in fear and hope) is causative (as a reason). It is also permissible for both to be verbal nouns in the accusative governed by an omitted verb.

**﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾.** The indefinite noun in the context of negation conveys generality. That is, no soul among souls, whichever soul it may be, knows what Allah, glorified is He, has hidden for those previously mentioned, of what will gladden their eyes. Al-Jumhur read *qurrati* in the singular. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah and Abu al-Darda' read *min qurrāt* in the plural. Hamzah read *mā ukhfiya* with a sukun on the yā', as an imperfect verb attributed to Allah, glorified is He. The rest read it with a fatḥah, as a passive past verb.

Ibn Mas'ud read *mā nukhfī* with a ḍammah on the nūn. Al-A'mash read *yukhfī* with a ḍammah on the yā' of the imperfect.

Al-Zajjaj said regarding the reading of Hamzah: the meaning is: some of what Allah has hidden for them. This is also the reading of Muhammad ibn Ka'b. The *mā* is in the accusative position.

Then, glorified is He, explained that this is because of their righteous deeds, saying: **﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾**, that is, for the sake of recompense for what they used to do in the world, or they are rewarded with that.

**﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiant?﴾** The interrogative is for denial, meaning: the believer is not like the defiant, for the difference between them has become clear. This is why He says, **﴿They are not equal﴾**. The plural form here is a further variation in expression of what the denial, conveyed by the interrogative, has conveyed. Al-Zajjaj said: He made two into a group when He said ﴿they are not equal﴾, because of the meaning of *min* (from, among). It is also said that it is because two is the least plural. The cause of its revelation will be explained at the end of the discussion.

Then, glorified is He, explained the outcome of the two groups, beginning with the believers, saying: **﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the gardens of refuge as a lodging﴾**. Al-Jumhur read *jannāt* in the plural. Talhah ibn Musarrif read *jannatu al-ma'wā* in the singular. *Al-ma'wā* is that to which they resort, and He attributed the gardens to it because it is the true refuge. It has also been said that *al-ma'wā* is one of the gardens, and this matter has been discussed earlier. The meaning of *nuzulan* (as a lodging/hospitality) is that they are prepared for them when they arrive. Originally it means what is prepared for the guest of food and drink, as we explained in Ali 'Imran. Its accusative is as a circumstantial clause.

Abu Haywah read *nuzlan* with a sukun on the zāy. The bā' in **﴿for what they used to do﴾** indicates causation, meaning: because of what they used to do, or because of their deeds.

Then He mentioned the other group, saying: **﴿As for those who defied﴾**, that is, departed from obedience to Allah and rebelled against Him and His messengers, **﴿their refuge is the Fire﴾**, that is, their abode to which they will go and in which they will settle is the Fire. **﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾**, that is, whenever they wish to leave it, they will be sent back into it, compelled and forced. It has also been said: when the flame pushes them to its top, they will be returned to their places. **﴿And it will be said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny"﴾**. The one who says this to them is the guardians of Hell from among the angels, or it is Allah, mighty and majestic. In this saying to them, while they are in the Fire, there is a degree of vexation to them that is not hidden.

**﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment﴾**, which is the punishment of the world.

Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak and al-Nakha'i said: it is the calamities of the world and its illnesses. It has also been said: the prescribed penalties (ḥudūd). It has been said: killing by the sword on the day of Badr. It has been said: the years of famine in Makkah. It has been said: the punishment of the grave. There is no barrier to taking all of these together. **﴿Short of the greater punishment﴾**, which is the punishment of the Hereafter, **﴿so that they may return﴾** from what they are in of shirk and sins, by means of what befalls them of punishment, to faith and obedience, and repent of what they were engaged in.

In this causal explanation there is evidence for the weakness of the view of those who said that the lesser punishment is the punishment of the grave.

**﴿And who is more unjust than one who was reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turned away from them?﴾**, that is, there is no one more unjust than him, because he heard from the signs of Allah what requires turning toward faith and obedience, but he substituted turning away in place of that. The bringing of *thumma* (then) is to indicate the improbability of this and that it is something which should not occur. **﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾**, that is, upon the people of crime in general, so that whoever turns away from the signs of Allah is included first and foremost.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words, **﴿We have forgotten you﴾**, that he said: "We have abandoned you."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab reported from him, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the five daily prayers: **﴿Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration﴾**, that is, they come to them, and glorify, that is, they pray by the command of their Lord, **﴿and they are not arrogant﴾** about performing the prayer in congregations.

Al-Tirmidhi related it and graded it sound (ṣaḥīḥ), as did Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Muhammad ibn Nasr in *Kitab al-Salat*, from Anas ibn Malik, that this verse, ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, was revealed concerning waiting for the prayer called *al-'Atamah* (the night prayer).

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, who said: It was revealed concerning the ʿIshaʾ prayer.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, also concerning the verse, that he said: They would not sleep until they had prayed the ʿIshaʾ.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from him, who said: We used to avoid bedding before the ʿIshaʾ prayer.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, in *al-Musannaf* (a collection of hadith arranged by topic), and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, also, who said: "I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sleeping before ʿIshaʾ, nor conversing after it, for this verse was revealed concerning that: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, [and] said: They are those who do not sleep before ʿIshaʾ, so he praised them."

When this was mentioned, a man began to leave his bed for fear that his eye would overcome him. Its time is before the child sleeps and the elderly become lax.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Bilal, who said: "We used to sit in the mosque while some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would pray the ʿIshaʾ after the Maghrib: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, Ibn ʿAdi, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, related from Anas regarding His saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, that he said: They used to wait between the Maghrib and the ʿIshaʾ, praying.

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, "from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, that he said: [It is] the standing of the servant in the night."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Nasr in *Kitab al-Salat*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* related from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned a long hadith in which he directed [the listener] to kinds of acts of obedience, and in it he said: "And a man's prayer in the depth of the night," then he recited: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), in a hadith in which he said: "And a man's prayer in the depth of the night," then he recited this verse.

Ibn Mardawayh also related from Anas concerning the verse, that he said: "There was no night that passed over them without them taking from it."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, related through Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Jadali, from ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, from Kaʿb, who said: "When people are gathered, a caller will call out: 'This is the Day of Judgment. Where are those whose sides forsake their beds?'" The hadith [continues].

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, that he said: [Their sides] forsake [their beds] for the remembrance of Allah. Whenever they awaken, they remember Allah, whether in prayer, or standing, or sitting, or on their sides; they never cease remembering Allah.

Al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Baʿth*, related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Throne of Allah was over the water. He made a garden for Himself, then made another beneath it, then sealed both with a single pearl. Then He said: ﴿And beneath them are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 62], without informing creation of what is in them. These are the ones of which Allah said: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾. Every day there comes to them from them a gift."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "Indeed, it is written in the Torah: 'Allah has prepared for those whose sides forsake their beds' what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human, nor does any near angel or sent prophet know it." And indeed it is in the Qur'an: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others related from Abu Hurayrah, "from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: Allah the Exalted said: 'I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human.'" Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾."

There are hadiths on this topic from a group of the Companions, and they are well known, so we will not lengthen by mentioning them.

Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani in *Kitab al-Aghani*, al-Wahidi, Ibn ʿAdi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn ʿAsakir related through various chains from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah said to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib: "I am sharper than you in spear-point, more active than you in tongue, and fuller for the battalion than you." ʿAli said to him: "Be silent, for you are only a fasiq (a wrongdoer)." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Is one who is a believer like one who is a wrongdoer? They are not equal﴾. By "the believer" is meant ʿAli, and by "the wrongdoer" al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt.

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn ʿAsakir related something similar from him concerning the verse.

Something similar was related from ʿAta' ibn Yasar, al-Suddi, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Mani', Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalail* related from Ibn Masʿud concerning His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste from the nearer punishment﴾, he said: "The Day of Badr." ﴿Short of the greater punishment﴾, he said: "The Day of Resurrection." ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾, he said: "Perhaps whoever remains of them will repent and return."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Masʿud concerning the verse, that he said: "The nearer punishment is years of drought that afflicted them. ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾: they will repent."

Muslim, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawaʾid al-Musnad*, Abu ʿAwanah in his *Sahih*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb concerning His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste from the nearer punishment﴾, that he said: "The calamities of this world, the Romans, the assault, and the smoke."

Ibn Jarir related from him, who said: "The Day of Badr."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿From the nearer punishment﴾, he said: "The prescribed penalties (ḥudūd)." ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾, he said: "They will repent."

Ibn Mani', Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh.

Al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain, from Muʿadh ibn Jabal: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever does three things has committed a crime: whoever ties a banner for an unjust cause, or disobeys his parents, or walks with an oppressor to support him, has indeed committed a crime." Allah says: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾.

Ibn Kathir said, after relating it: "This is a gharib (singular, weakly transmitted) hadith."

[p. 1151] **His words: ﴿Had you but seen the guilty, bowing their heads before their Lord﴾.** The "guilty" here are those who said, "When we have gone astray, shall we indeed be [brought back] anew?" The address is to anyone fit to receive it, or to the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ)).

It is also possible that "the guilty" refers to every guilty person, with those who made that statement included first and foremost. The phrase ﴿bowing their heads﴾ means lowering them in shame and remorse for what they committed in the world of shirk (association of partners with Allah) and disobedience to Him. The phrase ﴿before their Lord﴾ means at the time of His reckoning of them.

Al-Zajjaj said: The address to the Prophet (ﷺ) is an address to his community.
