The meaning is: "Had you seen, O Muhammad, the deniers of the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment, you would have seen a wondrous sight, [as they say,] ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾." That is, they say: "Our Lord, we now see what we used to deny, and we hear what we used to reject." It has also been said: "We have seen the truth of Your threat, and we have heard the confirmation of Your messengers." Thus these people saw when sight no longer benefited them, and heard when hearing no longer benefited them. ﴿So send us back﴾ to the world, "and we will do righteous deeds as You commanded us." ﴿Indeed, we are certain﴾, that is, affirming. It has also been said: affirming what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. They describe themselves as certain now, hoping for what they request, namely their return to the world. But how could that be? The word of Allah has already come due against them, for ﴿even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden, and they are indeed liars﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿we are certain﴾ is that the doubts which used to beset them in the world have now departed, since they have seen and heard what they have seen and heard. It is also possible that the meaning of ﴿we have seen and heard﴾ is "we have become among those who hear and see," so that there is no need to supply an object. It is also permissible for ﴿righteous﴾ (ṣāliḥan) to be the object of ﴿we will do﴾, just as it may be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The answer to ﴿Had you but seen﴾ (law, "had") is omitted, meaning: "you would have seen a dreadful matter and a terrifying horror."

**﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾.** This is a rebuttal of them when they asked for a return. That is: had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, guiding all people, so that none of them would have disbelieved.

Al-Nahhas said: Regarding the meaning of this there are two views: one is that it refers to the world, and the other is that it refers to the Hereafter. That is: had We willed, We would have sent them back to the world. ﴿But the word from Me has come due: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together﴾. The clause ﴿had We willed﴾ is understood as a clause introduced by a verb of saying, coordinated with what was understood before ﴿We have seen﴾, meaning: "and We say, had We willed..." The meaning of ﴿but the word from Me has come due﴾ is: My decree has taken effect, My predestination has been carried out, and My word has preceded. ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together﴾: this is the word that was decreed by Allah, became binding upon His servants, and whose decree took effect. The implication of this word is that He does not give every soul its guidance. He has decreed this against them because He, glorified is He, knew that they were of the wretched, and that they were among those who choose misguidance over guidance.

The fā' (so) in His words, ﴿So taste [the punishment] for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾, marks the order of the command to taste following what came before it. The bā' (for) in ﴿for having forgotten﴾ indicates causation, and it implies that their punishment is not merely due to the preceding decree, but to that and this together.

Scholars differed about the forgetting mentioned here. Some said it is genuine forgetting, the kind by which remembrance departs. Others said it is abandonment. According to the first view, the meaning is that they did not work for that Day, so they were like those who forget it and do not remember it. According to the second, a noun must be supplied before ﴿meeting﴾: "taste the punishment of the meeting of this your Day because of your abandonment of what you were commanded." Al-Mubarrad preferred the second view and recited:

*As if it were a skewer of a drinker, one who forgot it at the moment of its drawing out (?)* [He made the poem's point that forgetting means abandoning.]

That is, they abandoned it. Al-Dahhak and Yahya ibn Salam also said that forgetting here means abandoning. Yahya ibn Salam said: The meaning is: For having abandoned belief in the Resurrection on this Day, We abandon you from good. Al-Suddi said the same. Mujahid said: We abandon you in the punishment.

Muqatil said: When they enter the Fire, the guardians will say to them, "Taste the punishment for having forgotten." Here the word "taste" is used metaphorically for experiencing. Tufayl said:

*So taste as we tasted on the day of the ambush,*
*From the rage in our livers and the reproach.*

His words: ﴿And taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do﴾ are a repetition for emphasis. That is: taste the lasting punishment that never ends, for what you used to do in the world of disbelief and sins.

Al-Razi said in his Tafsir (exegesis): the demonstrative in His words, ﴿for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾, may have three possible referents: it may refer to the meeting, to the Day, or to the punishment.

The clause ﴿Only those believe in Our signs﴾ is a new sentence that explains who deserves guidance to belief and who does not. The meaning is: only those who affirm Our signs and benefit from them are ﴿those who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration﴾, and not others who are reminded of them, that is, admonished by them, but do not remember or believe in them. The phrase ﴿fall down in prostration﴾ means fall on their faces, prostrating, glorifying Allah's signs and fearing His might and punishment. ﴿And glorify their Lord with praise﴾, that is, they declare Him free of all that is unbefitting Him, while joined with praise for His blessings, the greatest and most complete of which is guidance to belief. The meaning is that they say in their prostration: "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," or "Glory be to my Lord the Most High and praise be to Him."

Sufyan said: The meaning is "pray out of praise for your Lord." The clause ﴿and they are not arrogant﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while they are humbly submissive to Allah, abasing themselves to Him, and not arrogant toward Him.

**﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾**, that is, they rise and lift themselves up. It is said: *jafā al-shay' 'an al-shay'* and *tajāfā 'anhu* when a thing does not cling to another and is set aside from it. ﴿Beds﴾ is the plural of *maḍja'* (bed), the place where one lies down. Al-Zajjaj and al-Rummani said: *tajāfī* and *tajaffī* are toward the upward direction, and likewise in pardoning the one who errs in abuse or the like. ﴿Sides﴾ is the plural of *janb*. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: their sides are forsaking their beds. These are those who pray at night (*mutahajjidūn*), who rise from their bedding for prayer. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ata', and the majority. The prayer intended is the voluntary night prayer (*tanafful*, supererogatory worship) without specification.

Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: it is voluntary prayer between Maghrib and 'Isha'. It has also been said: it is the 'Isha' prayer alone, a report from al-Hasan and 'Ata'. Al-Dahhak said: it is the 'Isha' and Fajr prayers in congregation. It has also been said: they are those who rise for the remembrance of Allah, whether in prayer or otherwise.

**﴿They call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾.** This clause is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, relating to the pronoun in ﴿their sides﴾. So it is a circumstantial clause following another circumstantial clause. It is also possible that the first clause is a new sentence explaining one kind of their acts of obedience. The meaning is: their sides forsake their beds while they call upon their Lord, fearing His punishment and hoping for His mercy.

**﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾**, that is, from what We have provided them, or from their provision. This is the obligatory charity. It has also been said: it is voluntary charity. The better view is to take it in general. The accusative of *khawfan wa-ṭam'an* (in fear and hope) is causative (as a reason). It is also permissible for both to be verbal nouns in the accusative governed by an omitted verb.

**﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾.** The indefinite noun in the context of negation conveys generality. That is, no soul among souls, whichever soul it may be, knows what Allah, glorified is He, has hidden for those previously mentioned, of what will gladden their eyes. Al-Jumhur read *qurrati* in the singular. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah and Abu al-Darda' read *min qurrāt* in the plural. Hamzah read *mā ukhfiya* with a sukun on the yā', as an imperfect verb attributed to Allah, glorified is He. The rest read it with a fatḥah, as a passive past verb.

Ibn Mas'ud read *mā nukhfī* with a ḍammah on the nūn. Al-A'mash read *yukhfī* with a ḍammah on the yā' of the imperfect.

Al-Zajjaj said regarding the reading of Hamzah: the meaning is: some of what Allah has hidden for them. This is also the reading of Muhammad ibn Ka'b. The *mā* is in the accusative position.

Then, glorified is He, explained that this is because of their righteous deeds, saying: **﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾**, that is, for the sake of recompense for what they used to do in the world, or they are rewarded with that.

**﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiant?﴾** The interrogative is for denial, meaning: the believer is not like the defiant, for the difference between them has become clear. This is why He says, **﴿They are not equal﴾**. The plural form here is a further variation in expression of what the denial, conveyed by the interrogative, has conveyed. Al-Zajjaj said: He made two into a group when He said ﴿they are not equal﴾, because of the meaning of *min* (from, among). It is also said that it is because two is the least plural. The cause of its revelation will be explained at the end of the discussion.

Then, glorified is He, explained the outcome of the two groups, beginning with the believers, saying: **﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the gardens of refuge as a lodging﴾**. Al-Jumhur read *jannāt* in the plural. Talhah ibn Musarrif read *jannatu al-ma'wā* in the singular. *Al-ma'wā* is that to which they resort, and He attributed the gardens to it because it is the true refuge. It has also been said that *al-ma'wā* is one of the gardens, and this matter has been discussed earlier. The meaning of *nuzulan* (as a lodging/hospitality) is that they are prepared for them when they arrive. Originally it means what is prepared for the guest of food and drink, as we explained in Ali 'Imran. Its accusative is as a circumstantial clause.

Abu Haywah read *nuzlan* with a sukun on the zāy. The bā' in **﴿for what they used to do﴾** indicates causation, meaning: because of what they used to do, or because of their deeds.

Then He mentioned the other group, saying: **﴿As for those who defied﴾**, that is, departed from obedience to Allah and rebelled against Him and His messengers, **﴿their refuge is the Fire﴾**, that is, their abode to which they will go and in which they will settle is the Fire. **﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾**, that is, whenever they wish to leave it, they will be sent back into it, compelled and forced. It has also been said: when the flame pushes them to its top, they will be returned to their places. **﴿And it will be said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny"﴾**. The one who says this to them is the guardians of Hell from among the angels, or it is Allah, mighty and majestic. In this saying to them, while they are in the Fire, there is a degree of vexation to them that is not hidden.

**﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment﴾**, which is the punishment of the world.

Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak and al-Nakha'i said: it is the calamities of the world and its illnesses. It has also been said: the prescribed penalties (ḥudūd). It has been said: killing by the sword on the day of Badr. It has been said: the years of famine in Makkah. It has been said: the punishment of the grave. There is no barrier to taking all of these together. **﴿Short of the greater punishment﴾**, which is the punishment of the Hereafter, **﴿so that they may return﴾** from what they are in of shirk and sins, by means of what befalls them of punishment, to faith and obedience, and repent of what they were engaged in.

In this causal explanation there is evidence for the weakness of the view of those who said that the lesser punishment is the punishment of the grave.

**﴿And who is more unjust than one who was reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turned away from them?﴾**, that is, there is no one more unjust than him, because he heard from the signs of Allah what requires turning toward faith and obedience, but he substituted turning away in place of that. The bringing of *thumma* (then) is to indicate the improbability of this and that it is something which should not occur. **﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾**, that is, upon the people of crime in general, so that whoever turns away from the signs of Allah is included first and foremost.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words, **﴿We have forgotten you﴾**, that he said: "We have abandoned you."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab reported from him, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the five daily prayers: **﴿Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration﴾**, that is, they come to them, and glorify, that is, they pray by the command of their Lord, **﴿and they are not arrogant﴾** about performing the prayer in congregations.

Al-Tirmidhi related it and graded it sound (ṣaḥīḥ), as did Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Muhammad ibn Nasr in *Kitab al-Salat*, from Anas ibn Malik, that this verse, ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, was revealed concerning waiting for the prayer called *al-'Atamah* (the night prayer).

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, who said: It was revealed concerning the ʿIshaʾ prayer.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, also concerning the verse, that he said: They would not sleep until they had prayed the ʿIshaʾ.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from him, who said: We used to avoid bedding before the ʿIshaʾ prayer.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, in *al-Musannaf* (a collection of hadith arranged by topic), and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, also, who said: "I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sleeping before ʿIshaʾ, nor conversing after it, for this verse was revealed concerning that: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, [and] said: They are those who do not sleep before ʿIshaʾ, so he praised them."

When this was mentioned, a man began to leave his bed for fear that his eye would overcome him. Its time is before the child sleeps and the elderly become lax.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Bilal, who said: "We used to sit in the mosque while some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would pray the ʿIshaʾ after the Maghrib: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, Ibn ʿAdi, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, related from Anas regarding His saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, that he said: They used to wait between the Maghrib and the ʿIshaʾ, praying.

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, "from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, that he said: [It is] the standing of the servant in the night."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Nasr in *Kitab al-Salat*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* related from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned a long hadith in which he directed [the listener] to kinds of acts of obedience, and in it he said: "And a man's prayer in the depth of the night," then he recited: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), in a hadith in which he said: "And a man's prayer in the depth of the night," then he recited this verse.

Ibn Mardawayh also related from Anas concerning the verse, that he said: "There was no night that passed over them without them taking from it."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, related through Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Jadali, from ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, from Kaʿb, who said: "When people are gathered, a caller will call out: 'This is the Day of Judgment. Where are those whose sides forsake their beds?'" The hadith [continues].

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, that he said: [Their sides] forsake [their beds] for the remembrance of Allah. Whenever they awaken, they remember Allah, whether in prayer, or standing, or sitting, or on their sides; they never cease remembering Allah.

Al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Baʿth*, related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Throne of Allah was over the water. He made a garden for Himself, then made another beneath it, then sealed both with a single pearl. Then He said: ﴿And beneath them are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 62], without informing creation of what is in them. These are the ones of which Allah said: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾. Every day there comes to them from them a gift."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "Indeed, it is written in the Torah: 'Allah has prepared for those whose sides forsake their beds' what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human, nor does any near angel or sent prophet know it." And indeed it is in the Qur'an: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others related from Abu Hurayrah, "from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: Allah the Exalted said: 'I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human.'" Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾."

There are hadiths on this topic from a group of the Companions, and they are well known, so we will not lengthen by mentioning them.

Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani in *Kitab al-Aghani*, al-Wahidi, Ibn ʿAdi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn ʿAsakir related through various chains from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah said to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib: "I am sharper than you in spear-point, more active than you in tongue, and fuller for the battalion than you." ʿAli said to him: "Be silent, for you are only a fasiq (a wrongdoer)." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Is one who is a believer like one who is a wrongdoer? They are not equal﴾. By "the believer" is meant ʿAli, and by "the wrongdoer" al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt.

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn ʿAsakir related something similar from him concerning the verse.

Something similar was related from ʿAta' ibn Yasar, al-Suddi, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Mani', Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalail* related from Ibn Masʿud concerning His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste from the nearer punishment﴾, he said: "The Day of Badr." ﴿Short of the greater punishment﴾, he said: "The Day of Resurrection." ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾, he said: "Perhaps whoever remains of them will repent and return."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Masʿud concerning the verse, that he said: "The nearer punishment is years of drought that afflicted them. ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾: they will repent."

Muslim, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawaʾid al-Musnad*, Abu ʿAwanah in his *Sahih*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb concerning His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste from the nearer punishment﴾, that he said: "The calamities of this world, the Romans, the assault, and the smoke."

Ibn Jarir related from him, who said: "The Day of Badr."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿From the nearer punishment﴾, he said: "The prescribed penalties (ḥudūd)." ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾, he said: "They will repent."

Ibn Mani', Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh.

Al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain, from Muʿadh ibn Jabal: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever does three things has committed a crime: whoever ties a banner for an unjust cause, or disobeys his parents, or walks with an oppressor to support him, has indeed committed a crime." Allah says: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾.

Ibn Kathir said, after relating it: "This is a gharib (singular, weakly transmitted) hadith."

[p. 1151] **His words: ﴿Had you but seen the guilty, bowing their heads before their Lord﴾.** The "guilty" here are those who said, "When we have gone astray, shall we indeed be [brought back] anew?" The address is to anyone fit to receive it, or to the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ)).

It is also possible that "the guilty" refers to every guilty person, with those who made that statement included first and foremost. The phrase ﴿bowing their heads﴾ means lowering them in shame and remorse for what they committed in the world of shirk (association of partners with Allah) and disobedience to Him. The phrase ﴿before their Lord﴾ means at the time of His reckoning of them.

Al-Zajjaj said: The address to the Prophet (ﷺ) is an address to his community. The meaning is: "Had you seen, O Muhammad, the deniers of the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment, you would have seen a wondrous sight, [as they say,] ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾." That is, they say: "Our Lord, we now see what we used to deny, and we hear what we used to reject." It has also been said: "We have seen the truth of Your threat, and we have heard the confirmation of Your messengers." Thus these people saw when sight no longer benefited them, and heard when hearing no longer benefited them. ﴿So send us back﴾ to the world, "and we will do righteous deeds as You commanded us." ﴿Indeed, we are certain﴾, that is, affirming. It has also been said: affirming what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. They describe themselves as certain now, hoping for what they request, namely their return to the world. But how could that be? The word of Allah has already come due against them, for ﴿even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden, and they are indeed liars﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿we are certain﴾ is that the doubts which used to beset them in the world have now departed, since they have seen and heard what they have seen and heard. It is also possible that the meaning of ﴿we have seen and heard﴾ is "we have become among those who hear and see," so that there is no need to supply an object. It is also permissible for ﴿righteous﴾ (ṣāliḥan) to be the object of ﴿we will do﴾, just as it may be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The answer to ﴿Had you but seen﴾ (law, "had") is omitted, meaning: "you would have seen a dreadful matter and a terrifying horror."

**﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾.** This is a rebuttal of them when they asked for a return. That is: had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, guiding all people, so that none of them would have disbelieved.

Al-Nahhas said: Regarding the meaning of this there are two views: one is that it refers to the world, and the other is that it refers to the Hereafter. That is: had We willed, We would have sent them back to the world. ﴿But the word from Me has come due: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together﴾. The clause ﴿had We willed﴾ is understood as a clause introduced by a verb of saying, coordinated with what was understood before ﴿We have seen﴾, meaning: "and We say, had We willed..." The meaning of ﴿but the word from Me has come due﴾ is: My decree has taken effect, My predestination has been carried out, and My word has preceded. ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together﴾: this is the word that was decreed by Allah, became binding upon His servants, and whose decree took effect. The implication of this word is that He does not give every soul its guidance. He has decreed this against them because He, glorified is He, knew that they were of the wretched, and that they were among those who choose misguidance over guidance.

The fā' (so) in His words, ﴿So taste [the punishment] for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾, marks the order of the command to taste following what came before it. The bā' (for) in ﴿for having forgotten﴾ indicates causation, and it implies that their punishment is not merely due to the preceding decree, but to that and this together.

Scholars differed about the forgetting mentioned here. Some said it is genuine forgetting, the kind by which remembrance departs. Others said it is abandonment. According to the first view, the meaning is that they did not work for that Day, so they were like those who forget it and do not remember it. According to the second, a noun must be supplied before ﴿meeting﴾: "taste the punishment of the meeting of this your Day because of your abandonment of what you were commanded." Al-Mubarrad preferred the second view and recited:

*As if it were a skewer of a drinker, one who forgot it at the moment of its drawing out (?)* [He made the poem's point that forgetting means abandoning.]

That is, they abandoned it. Al-Dahhak and Yahya ibn Salam also said that forgetting here means abandoning. Yahya ibn Salam said: The meaning is: For having abandoned belief in the Resurrection on this Day, We abandon you from good. Al-Suddi said the same. Mujahid said: We abandon you in the punishment.

Muqatil said: When they enter the Fire, the guardians will say to them, "Taste the punishment for having forgotten." Here the word "taste" is used metaphorically for experiencing. Tufayl said:

*So taste as we tasted on the day of the ambush,*
*From the rage in our livers and the reproach.*

His words: ﴿And taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do﴾ are a repetition for emphasis. That is: taste the lasting punishment that never ends, for what you used to do in the world of disbelief and sins.

Al-Razi said in his Tafsir (exegesis): the demonstrative in His words, ﴿for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾, may have three possible referents: it may refer to the meeting, to the Day, or to the punishment.

The clause ﴿Only those believe in Our signs﴾ is a new sentence that explains who deserves guidance to belief and who does not. The meaning is: only those who affirm Our signs and benefit from them are ﴿those who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration﴾, and not others who are reminded of them, that is, admonished by them, but do not remember or believe in them. The phrase ﴿fall down in prostration﴾ means fall on their faces, prostrating, glorifying Allah's signs and fearing His might and punishment. ﴿And glorify their Lord with praise﴾, that is, they declare Him free of all that is unbefitting Him, while joined with praise for His blessings, the greatest and most complete of which is guidance to belief. The meaning is that they say in their prostration: "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," or "Glory be to my Lord the Most High and praise be to Him."

Sufyan said: The meaning is "pray out of praise for your Lord." The clause ﴿and they are not arrogant﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while they are humbly submissive to Allah, abasing themselves to Him, and not arrogant toward Him.

**﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾**, that is, they rise and lift themselves up. It is said: *jafā al-shay' 'an al-shay'* and *tajāfā 'anhu* when a thing does not cling to another and is set aside from it. ﴿Beds﴾ is the plural of *maḍja'* (bed), the place where one lies down. Al-Zajjaj and al-Rummani said: *tajāfī* and *tajaffī* are toward the upward direction, and likewise in pardoning the one who errs in abuse or the like. ﴿Sides﴾ is the plural of *janb*. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: their sides are forsaking their beds. These are those who pray at night (*mutahajjidūn*), who rise from their bedding for prayer. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ata', and the majority. The prayer intended is the voluntary night prayer (*tanafful*, supererogatory worship) without specification.

Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: it is voluntary prayer between Maghrib and 'Isha'. It has also been said: it is the 'Isha' prayer alone, a report from al-Hasan and 'Ata'. Al-Dahhak said: it is the 'Isha' and Fajr prayers in congregation. It has also been said: they are those who rise for the remembrance of Allah, whether in prayer or otherwise.

**﴿They call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾.** This clause is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, relating to the pronoun in ﴿their sides﴾. So it is a circumstantial clause following another circumstantial clause. It is also possible that the first clause is a new sentence explaining one kind of their acts of obedience. The meaning is: their sides forsake their beds while they call upon their Lord, fearing His punishment and hoping for His mercy.

**﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾**, that is, from what We have provided them, or from their provision. This is the obligatory charity. It has also been said: it is voluntary charity. The better view is to take it in general. The accusative of *khawfan wa-ṭam'an* (in fear and hope) is causative (as a reason). It is also permissible for both to be verbal nouns in the accusative governed by an omitted verb.

**﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾.** The indefinite noun in the context of negation conveys generality. That is, no soul among souls, whichever soul it may be, knows what Allah, glorified is He, has hidden for those previously mentioned, of what will gladden their eyes. Al-Jumhur read *qurrati* in the singular. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah and Abu al-Darda' read *min qurrāt* in the plural. Hamzah read *mā ukhfiya* with a sukun on the yā', as an imperfect verb attributed to Allah, glorified is He. The rest read it with a fatḥah, as a passive past verb.

Ibn Mas'ud read *mā nukhfī* with a ḍammah on the nūn. Al-A'mash read *yukhfī* with a ḍammah on the yā' of the imperfect.

Al-Zajjaj said regarding the reading of Hamzah: the meaning is: some of what Allah has hidden for them. This is also the reading of Muhammad ibn Ka'b. The *mā* is in the accusative position.

Then, glorified is He, explained that this is because of their righteous deeds, saying: **﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾**, that is, for the sake of recompense for what they used to do in the world, or they are rewarded with that.

**﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiant?﴾** The interrogative is for denial, meaning: the believer is not like the defiant, for the difference between them has become clear. This is why He says, **﴿They are not equal﴾**. The plural form here is a further variation in expression of what the denial, conveyed by the interrogative, has conveyed. Al-Zajjaj said: He made two into a group when He said ﴿they are not equal﴾, because of the meaning of *min* (from, among). It is also said that it is because two is the least plural. The cause of its revelation will be explained at the end of the discussion.

Then, glorified is He, explained the outcome of the two groups, beginning with the believers, saying: **﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the gardens of refuge as a lodging﴾**. Al-Jumhur read *jannāt* in the plural. Talhah ibn Musarrif read *jannatu al-ma'wā* in the singular. *Al-ma'wā* is that to which they resort, and He attributed the gardens to it because it is the true refuge. It has also been said that *al-ma'wā* is one of the gardens, and this matter has been discussed earlier. The meaning of *nuzulan* (as a lodging/hospitality) is that they are prepared for them when they arrive. Originally it means what is prepared for the guest of food and drink, as we explained in Ali 'Imran. Its accusative is as a circumstantial clause.

Abu Haywah read *nuzlan* with a sukun on the zāy. The bā' in **﴿for what they used to do﴾** indicates causation, meaning: because of what they used to do, or because of their deeds.

Then He mentioned the other group, saying: **﴿As for those who defied﴾**, that is, departed from obedience to Allah and rebelled against Him and His messengers, **﴿their refuge is the Fire﴾**, that is, their abode to which they will go and in which they will settle is the Fire. **﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾**, that is, whenever they wish to leave it, they will be sent back into it, compelled and forced. It has also been said: when the flame pushes them to its top, they will be returned to their places. **﴿And it will be said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny"﴾**. The one who says this to them is the guardians of Hell from among the angels, or it is Allah, mighty and majestic. In this saying to them, while they are in the Fire, there is a degree of vexation to them that is not hidden.

**﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment﴾**, which is the punishment of the world.

Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak and al-Nakha'i said: it is the calamities of the world and its illnesses. It has also been said: the prescribed penalties (ḥudūd). It has been said: killing by the sword on the day of Badr. It has been said: the years of famine in Makkah. It has been said: the punishment of the grave. There is no barrier to taking all of these together. **﴿Short of the greater punishment﴾**, which is the punishment of the Hereafter, **﴿so that they may return﴾** from what they are in of shirk and sins, by means of what befalls them of punishment, to faith and obedience, and repent of what they were engaged in.

In this causal explanation there is evidence for the weakness of the view of those who said that the lesser punishment is the punishment of the grave.

**﴿And who is more unjust than one who was reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turned away from them?﴾**, that is, there is no one more unjust than him, because he heard from the signs of Allah what requires turning toward faith and obedience, but he substituted turning away in place of that. The bringing of *thumma* (then) is to indicate the improbability of this and that it is something which should not occur. **﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾**, that is, upon the people of crime in general, so that whoever turns away from the signs of Allah is included first and foremost.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words, **﴿We have forgotten you﴾**, that he said: "We have abandoned you."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab reported from him, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the five daily prayers: **﴿Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration﴾**, that is, they come to them, and glorify, that is, they pray by the command of their Lord, **﴿and they are not arrogant﴾** about performing the prayer in congregations.

Al-Tirmidhi related it and graded it sound (ṣaḥīḥ), as did Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Muhammad ibn Nasr in *Kitab al-Salat*, from Anas ibn Malik, that this verse, ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, was revealed concerning waiting for the prayer called *al-'Atamah* (the night prayer).

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, who said: It was revealed concerning the ʿIshaʾ prayer.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, also concerning the verse, that he said: They would not sleep until they had prayed the ʿIshaʾ.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from him, who said: We used to avoid bedding before the ʿIshaʾ prayer.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, in *al-Musannaf* (a collection of hadith arranged by topic), and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, also, who said: "I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sleeping before ʿIshaʾ, nor conversing after it, for this verse was revealed concerning that: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, [and] said: They are those who do not sleep before ʿIshaʾ, so he praised them."

When this was mentioned, a man began to leave his bed for fear that his eye would overcome him. Its time is before the child sleeps and the elderly become lax.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Bilal, who said: "We used to sit in the mosque while some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would pray the ʿIshaʾ after the Maghrib: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, Ibn ʿAdi, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, related from Anas regarding His saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, that he said: They used to wait between the Maghrib and the ʿIshaʾ, praying.

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, "from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, that he said: [It is] the standing of the servant in the night."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Nasr in *Kitab al-Salat*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* related from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned a long hadith in which he directed [the listener] to kinds of acts of obedience, and in it he said: "And a man's prayer in the depth of the night," then he recited: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), in a hadith in which he said: "And a man's prayer in the depth of the night," then he recited this verse.

Ibn Mardawayh also related from Anas concerning the verse, that he said: "There was no night that passed over them without them taking from it."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, related through Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Jadali, from ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, from Kaʿb, who said: "When people are gathered, a caller will call out: 'This is the Day of Judgment. Where are those whose sides forsake their beds?'" The hadith [continues].

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, that he said: [Their sides] forsake [their beds] for the remembrance of Allah. Whenever they awaken, they remember Allah, whether in prayer, or standing, or sitting, or on their sides; they never cease remembering Allah.

Al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Baʿth*, related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Throne of Allah was over the water. He made a garden for Himself, then made another beneath it, then sealed both with a single pearl. Then He said: ﴿And beneath them are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 62], without informing creation of what is in them. These are the ones of which Allah said: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾. Every day there comes to them from them a gift."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "Indeed, it is written in the Torah: 'Allah has prepared for those whose sides forsake their beds' what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human, nor does any near angel or sent prophet know it." And indeed it is in the Qur'an: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others related from Abu Hurayrah, "from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: Allah the Exalted said: 'I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human.'" Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾."

There are hadiths on this topic from a group of the Companions, and they are well known, so we will not lengthen by mentioning them.

Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani in *Kitab al-Aghani*, al-Wahidi, Ibn ʿAdi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn ʿAsakir related through various chains from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah said to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib: "I am sharper than you in spear-point, more active than you in tongue, and fuller for the battalion than you." ʿAli said to him: "Be silent, for you are only a fasiq (a wrongdoer)." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Is one who is a believer like one who is a wrongdoer? They are not equal﴾. By "the believer" is meant ʿAli, and by "the wrongdoer" al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt.

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn ʿAsakir related something similar from him concerning the verse.

Something similar was related from ʿAta' ibn Yasar, al-Suddi, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Mani', Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalail* related from Ibn Masʿud concerning His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste from the nearer punishment﴾, he said: "The Day of Badr." ﴿Short of the greater punishment﴾, he said: "The Day of Resurrection." ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾, he said: "Perhaps whoever remains of them will repent and return."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Masʿud concerning the verse, that he said: "The nearer punishment is years of drought that afflicted them. ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾: they will repent."

Muslim, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawaʾid al-Musnad*, Abu ʿAwanah in his *Sahih*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb concerning His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste from the nearer punishment﴾, that he said: "The calamities of this world, the Romans, the assault, and the smoke."

Ibn Jarir related from him, who said: "The Day of Badr."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿From the nearer punishment﴾, he said: "The prescribed penalties (ḥudūd)." ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾, he said: "They will repent."

Ibn Mani', Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh.

Al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain, from Muʿadh ibn Jabal: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever does three things has committed a crime: whoever ties a banner for an unjust cause, or disobeys his parents, or walks with an oppressor to support him, has indeed committed a crime." Allah says: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾.

Ibn Kathir said, after relating it: "This is a gharib (singular, weakly transmitted) hadith."

[p. 1151] **His words: ﴿Had you but seen the guilty, bowing their heads before their Lord﴾.** The "guilty" here are those who said, "When we have gone astray, shall we indeed be [brought back] anew?" The address is to anyone fit to receive it, or to the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ)).

It is also possible that "the guilty" refers to every guilty person, with those who made that statement included first and foremost. The phrase ﴿bowing their heads﴾ means lowering them in shame and remorse for what they committed in the world of shirk (association of partners with Allah) and disobedience to Him. The phrase ﴿before their Lord﴾ means at the time of His reckoning of them.

Al-Zajjaj said: The address to the Prophet (ﷺ) is an address to his community. The meaning is: "Had you seen, O Muhammad, the deniers of the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment, you would have seen a wondrous sight, [as they say,] ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾." That is, they say: "Our Lord, we now see what we used to deny, and we hear what we used to reject." It has also been said: "We have seen the truth of Your threat, and we have heard the confirmation of Your messengers." Thus these people saw when sight no longer benefited them, and heard when hearing no longer benefited them. ﴿So send us back﴾ to the world, "and we will do righteous deeds as You commanded us." ﴿Indeed, we are certain﴾, that is, affirming. It has also been said: affirming what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. They describe themselves as certain now, hoping for what they request, namely their return to the world. But how could that be? The word of Allah has already come due against them, for ﴿even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden, and they are indeed liars﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿we are certain﴾ is that the doubts which used to beset them in the world have now departed, since they have seen and heard what they have seen and heard. It is also possible that the meaning of ﴿we have seen and heard﴾ is "we have become among those who hear and see," so that there is no need to supply an object. It is also permissible for ﴿righteous﴾ (ṣāliḥan) to be the object of ﴿we will do﴾, just as it may be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The answer to ﴿Had you but seen﴾ (law, "had") is omitted, meaning: "you would have seen a dreadful matter and a terrifying horror."

**﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾.** This is a rebuttal of them when they asked for a return. That is: had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, guiding all people, so that none of them would have disbelieved.

Al-Nahhas said: Regarding the meaning of this there are two views: one is that it refers to the world, and the other is that it refers to the Hereafter. That is: had We willed, We would have sent them back to the world. ﴿But the word from Me has come due: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together﴾. The clause ﴿had We willed﴾ is understood as a clause introduced by a verb of saying, coordinated with what was understood before ﴿We have seen﴾, meaning: "and We say, had We willed..." The meaning of ﴿but the word from Me has come due﴾ is: My decree has taken effect, My predestination has been carried out, and My word has preceded. ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together﴾: this is the word that was decreed by Allah, became binding upon His servants, and whose decree took effect. The implication of this word is that He does not give every soul its guidance. He has decreed this against them because He, glorified is He, knew that they were of the wretched, and that they were among those who choose misguidance over guidance.

The fā' (so) in His words, ﴿So taste [the punishment] for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾, marks the order of the command to taste following what came before it. The bā' (for) in ﴿for having forgotten﴾ indicates causation, and it implies that their punishment is not merely due to the preceding decree, but to that and this together.

Scholars differed about the forgetting mentioned here. Some said it is genuine forgetting, the kind by which remembrance departs. Others said it is abandonment. According to the first view, the meaning is that they did not work for that Day, so they were like those who forget it and do not remember it. According to the second, a noun must be supplied before ﴿meeting﴾: "taste the punishment of the meeting of this your Day because of your abandonment of what you were commanded." Al-Mubarrad preferred the second view and recited:

*As if it were a skewer of a drinker, one who forgot it at the moment of its drawing out (?)* [He made the poem's point that forgetting means abandoning.]

That is, they abandoned it. Al-Dahhak and Yahya ibn Salam also said that forgetting here means abandoning. Yahya ibn Salam said: The meaning is: For having abandoned belief in the Resurrection on this Day, We abandon you from good. Al-Suddi said the same. Mujahid said: We abandon you in the punishment.

Muqatil said: When they enter the Fire, the guardians will say to them, "Taste the punishment for having forgotten." Here the word "taste" is used metaphorically for experiencing. Tufayl said:

*So taste as we tasted on the day of the ambush,*
*From the rage in our livers and the reproach.*

His words: ﴿And taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do﴾ are a repetition for emphasis. That is: taste the lasting punishment that never ends, for what you used to do in the world of disbelief and sins.

Al-Razi said in his Tafsir (exegesis): the demonstrative in His words, ﴿for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾, may have three possible referents: it may refer to the meeting, to the Day, or to the punishment.

The clause ﴿Only those believe in Our signs﴾ is a new sentence that explains who deserves guidance to belief and who does not. The meaning is: only those who affirm Our signs and benefit from them are ﴿those who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration﴾, and not others who are reminded of them, that is, admonished by them, but do not remember or believe in them. The phrase ﴿fall down in prostration﴾ means fall on their faces, prostrating, glorifying Allah's signs and fearing His might and punishment. ﴿And glorify their Lord with praise﴾, that is, they declare Him free of all that is unbefitting Him, while joined with praise for His blessings, the greatest and most complete of which is guidance to belief. The meaning is that they say in their prostration: "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," or "Glory be to my Lord the Most High and praise be to Him."

Sufyan said: The meaning is "pray out of praise for your Lord." The clause ﴿and they are not arrogant﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while they are humbly submissive to Allah, abasing themselves to Him, and not arrogant toward Him.

**﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾**, that is, they rise and lift themselves up. It is said: *jafā al-shay' 'an al-shay'* and *tajāfā 'anhu* when a thing does not cling to another and is set aside from it. ﴿Beds﴾ is the plural of *maḍja'* (bed), the place where one lies down. Al-Zajjaj and al-Rummani said: *tajāfī* and *tajaffī* are toward the upward direction, and likewise in pardoning the one who errs in abuse or the like. ﴿Sides﴾ is the plural of *janb*. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: their sides are forsaking their beds. These are those who pray at night (*mutahajjidūn*), who rise from their bedding for prayer. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ata', and the majority. The prayer intended is the voluntary night prayer (*tanafful*, supererogatory worship) without specification.

Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: it is voluntary prayer between Maghrib and 'Isha'. It has also been said: it is the 'Isha' prayer alone, a report from al-Hasan and 'Ata'. Al-Dahhak said: it is the 'Isha' and Fajr prayers in congregation. It has also been said: they are those who rise for the remembrance of Allah, whether in prayer or otherwise.

**﴿They call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾.** This clause is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, relating to the pronoun in ﴿their sides﴾. So it is a circumstantial clause following another circumstantial clause. It is also possible that the first clause is a new sentence explaining one kind of their acts of obedience. The meaning is: their sides forsake their beds while they call upon their Lord, fearing His punishment and hoping for His mercy.

**﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾**, that is, from what We have provided them, or from their provision. This is the obligatory charity. It has also been said: it is voluntary charity. The better view is to take it in general. The accusative of *khawfan wa-ṭam'an* (in fear and hope) is causative (as a reason). It is also permissible for both to be verbal nouns in the accusative governed by an omitted verb.

**﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾.** The indefinite noun in the context of negation conveys generality. That is, no soul among souls, whichever soul it may be, knows what Allah, glorified is He, has hidden for those previously mentioned, of what will gladden their eyes. Al-Jumhur read *qurrati* in the singular. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah and Abu al-Darda' read *min qurrāt* in the plural. Hamzah read *mā ukhfiya* with a sukun on the yā', as an imperfect verb attributed to Allah, glorified is He. The rest read it with a fatḥah, as a passive past verb.

Ibn Mas'ud read *mā nukhfī* with a ḍammah on the nūn. Al-A'mash read *yukhfī* with a ḍammah on the yā' of the imperfect.

Al-Zajjaj said regarding the reading of Hamzah: the meaning is: some of what Allah has hidden for them. This is also the reading of Muhammad ibn Ka'b. The *mā* is in the accusative position.

Then, glorified is He, explained that this is because of their righteous deeds, saying: **﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾**, that is, for the sake of recompense for what they used to do in the world, or they are rewarded with that.

**﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiant?﴾** The interrogative is for denial, meaning: the believer is not like the defiant, for the difference between them has become clear. This is why He says, **﴿They are not equal﴾**. The plural form here is a further variation in expression of what the denial, conveyed by the interrogative, has conveyed. Al-Zajjaj said: He made two into a group when He said ﴿they are not equal﴾, because of the meaning of *min* (from, among). It is also said that it is because two is the least plural. The cause of its revelation will be explained at the end of the discussion.

Then, glorified is He, explained the outcome of the two groups, beginning with the believers, saying: **﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the gardens of refuge as a lodging﴾**. Al-Jumhur read *jannāt* in the plural. Talhah ibn Musarrif read *jannatu al-ma'wā* in the singular. *Al-ma'wā* is that to which they resort, and He attributed the gardens to it because it is the true refuge. It has also been said that *al-ma'wā* is one of the gardens, and this matter has been discussed earlier. The meaning of *nuzulan* (as a lodging/hospitality) is that they are prepared for them when they arrive. Originally it means what is prepared for the guest of food and drink, as we explained in Ali 'Imran. Its accusative is as a circumstantial clause.

Abu Haywah read *nuzlan* with a sukun on the zāy. The bā' in **﴿for what they used to do﴾** indicates causation, meaning: because of what they used to do, or because of their deeds.

Then He mentioned the other group, saying: **﴿As for those who defied﴾**, that is, departed from obedience to Allah and rebelled against Him and His messengers, **﴿their refuge is the Fire﴾**, that is, their abode to which they will go and in which they will settle is the Fire. **﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾**, that is, whenever they wish to leave it, they will be sent back into it, compelled and forced. It has also been said: when the flame pushes them to its top, they will be returned to their places. **﴿And it will be said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny"﴾**. The one who says this to them is the guardians of Hell from among the angels, or it is Allah, mighty and majestic. In this saying to them, while they are in the Fire, there is a degree of vexation to them that is not hidden.

**﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment﴾**, which is the punishment of the world.

Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak and al-Nakha'i said: it is the calamities of the world and its illnesses. It has also been said: the prescribed penalties (ḥudūd). It has been said: killing by the sword on the day of Badr. It has been said: the years of famine in Makkah. It has been said: the punishment of the grave. There is no barrier to taking all of these together. **﴿Short of the greater punishment﴾**, which is the punishment of the Hereafter, **﴿so that they may return﴾** from what they are in of shirk and sins, by means of what befalls them of punishment, to faith and obedience, and repent of what they were engaged in.

In this causal explanation there is evidence for the weakness of the view of those who said that the lesser punishment is the punishment of the grave.

**﴿And who is more unjust than one who was reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turned away from them?﴾**, that is, there is no one more unjust than him, because he heard from the signs of Allah what requires turning toward faith and obedience, but he substituted turning away in place of that. The bringing of *thumma* (then) is to indicate the improbability of this and that it is something which should not occur. **﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾**, that is, upon the people of crime in general, so that whoever turns away from the signs of Allah is included first and foremost.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words, **﴿We have forgotten you﴾**, that he said: "We have abandoned you."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab reported from him, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the five daily prayers: **﴿Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration﴾**, that is, they come to them, and glorify, that is, they pray by the command of their Lord, **﴿and they are not arrogant﴾** about performing the prayer in congregations.

Al-Tirmidhi related it and graded it sound (ṣaḥīḥ), as did Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Muhammad ibn Nasr in *Kitab al-Salat*, from Anas ibn Malik, that this verse, ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, was revealed concerning waiting for the prayer called *al-'Atamah* (the night prayer).

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, who said: It was revealed concerning the ʿIshaʾ prayer.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, also concerning the verse, that he said: They would not sleep until they had prayed the ʿIshaʾ.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from him, who said: We used to avoid bedding before the ʿIshaʾ prayer.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, in *al-Musannaf* (a collection of hadith arranged by topic), and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, also, who said: "I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sleeping before ʿIshaʾ, nor conversing after it, for this verse was revealed concerning that: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, [and] said: They are those who do not sleep before ʿIshaʾ, so he praised them."

When this was mentioned, a man began to leave his bed for fear that his eye would overcome him. Its time is before the child sleeps and the elderly become lax.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Bilal, who said: "We used to sit in the mosque while some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would pray the ʿIshaʾ after the Maghrib: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, Ibn ʿAdi, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, related from Anas regarding His saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, that he said: They used to wait between the Maghrib and the ʿIshaʾ, praying.

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, "from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, that he said: [It is] the standing of the servant in the night."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Nasr in *Kitab al-Salat*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* related from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned a long hadith in which he directed [the listener] to kinds of acts of obedience, and in it he said: "And a man's prayer in the depth of the night," then he recited: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), in a hadith in which he said: "And a man's prayer in the depth of the night," then he recited this verse.

Ibn Mardawayh also related from Anas concerning the verse, that he said: "There was no night that passed over them without them taking from it."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, related through Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Jadali, from ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, from Kaʿb, who said: "When people are gathered, a caller will call out: 'This is the Day of Judgment. Where are those whose sides forsake their beds?'" The hadith [continues].

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, that he said: [Their sides] forsake [their beds] for the remembrance of Allah. Whenever they awaken, they remember Allah, whether in prayer, or standing, or sitting, or on their sides; they never cease remembering Allah.

Al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Baʿth*, related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Throne of Allah was over the water. He made a garden for Himself, then made another beneath it, then sealed both with a single pearl. Then He said: ﴿And beneath them are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 62], without informing creation of what is in them. These are the ones of which Allah said: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾. Every day there comes to them from them a gift."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "Indeed, it is written in the Torah: 'Allah has prepared for those whose sides forsake their beds' what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human, nor does any near angel or sent prophet know it." And indeed it is in the Qur'an: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others related from Abu Hurayrah, "from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: Allah the Exalted said: 'I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human.'" Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾."

There are hadiths on this topic from a group of the Companions, and they are well known, so we will not lengthen by mentioning them.

Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani in *Kitab al-Aghani*, al-Wahidi, Ibn ʿAdi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn ʿAsakir related through various chains from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah said to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib: "I am sharper than you in spear-point, more active than you in tongue, and fuller for the battalion than you." ʿAli said to him: "Be silent, for you are only a fasiq (a wrongdoer)." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Is one who is a believer like one who is a wrongdoer? They are not equal﴾. By "the believer" is meant ʿAli, and by "the wrongdoer" al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt.

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn ʿAsakir related something similar from him concerning the verse.

Something similar was related from ʿAta' ibn Yasar, al-Suddi, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Mani', Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalail* related from Ibn Masʿud concerning His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste from the nearer punishment﴾, he said: "The Day of Badr." ﴿Short of the greater punishment﴾, he said: "The Day of Resurrection." ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾, he said: "Perhaps whoever remains of them will repent and return."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Masʿud concerning the verse, that he said: "The nearer punishment is years of drought that afflicted them. ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾: they will repent."

Muslim, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawaʾid al-Musnad*, Abu ʿAwanah in his *Sahih*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb concerning His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste from the nearer punishment﴾, that he said: "The calamities of this world, the Romans, the assault, and the smoke."

Ibn Jarir related from him, who said: "The Day of Badr."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿From the nearer punishment﴾, he said: "The prescribed penalties (ḥudūd)." ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾, he said: "They will repent."

Ibn Mani', Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh.

Al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain, from Muʿadh ibn Jabal: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever does three things has committed a crime: whoever ties a banner for an unjust cause, or disobeys his parents, or walks with an oppressor to support him, has indeed committed a crime." Allah says: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾.

Ibn Kathir said, after relating it: "This is a gharib (singular, weakly transmitted) hadith."

[p. 1151] **His words: ﴿Had you but seen the guilty, bowing their heads before their Lord﴾.** The "guilty" here are those who said, "When we have gone astray, shall we indeed be [brought back] anew?" The address is to anyone fit to receive it, or to the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ)).

It is also possible that "the guilty" refers to every guilty person, with those who made that statement included first and foremost. The phrase ﴿bowing their heads﴾ means lowering them in shame and remorse for what they committed in the world of shirk (association of partners with Allah) and disobedience to Him. The phrase ﴿before their Lord﴾ means at the time of His reckoning of them.

Al-Zajjaj said: The address to the Prophet (ﷺ) is an address to his community. The meaning is: "Had you seen, O Muhammad, the deniers of the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment, you would have seen a wondrous sight, [as they say,] ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾." That is, they say: "Our Lord, we now see what we used to deny, and we hear what we used to reject." It has also been said: "We have seen the truth of Your threat, and we have heard the confirmation of Your messengers." Thus these people saw when sight no longer benefited them, and heard when hearing no longer benefited them. ﴿So send us back﴾ to the world, "and we will do righteous deeds as You commanded us." ﴿Indeed, we are certain﴾, that is, affirming. It has also been said: affirming what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. They describe themselves as certain now, hoping for what they request, namely their return to the world. But how could that be? The word of Allah has already come due against them, for ﴿even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden, and they are indeed liars﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿we are certain﴾ is that the doubts which used to beset them in the world have now departed, since they have seen and heard what they have seen and heard. It is also possible that the meaning of ﴿we have seen and heard﴾ is "we have become among those who hear and see," so that there is no need to supply an object. It is also permissible for ﴿righteous﴾ (ṣāliḥan) to be the object of ﴿we will do﴾, just as it may be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The answer to ﴿Had you but seen﴾ (law, "had") is omitted, meaning: "you would have seen a dreadful matter and a terrifying horror."

**﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾.** This is a rebuttal of them when they asked for a return. That is: had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, guiding all people, so that none of them would have disbelieved.

Al-Nahhas said: Regarding the meaning of this there are two views: one is that it refers to the world, and the other is that it refers to the Hereafter. That is: had We willed, We would have sent them back to the world. ﴿But the word from Me has come due: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together﴾. The clause ﴿had We willed﴾ is understood as a clause introduced by a verb of saying, coordinated with what was understood before ﴿We have seen﴾, meaning: "and We say, had We willed..." The meaning of ﴿but the word from Me has come due﴾ is: My decree has taken effect, My predestination has been carried out, and My word has preceded. ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together﴾: this is the word that was decreed by Allah, became binding upon His servants, and whose decree took effect. The implication of this word is that He does not give every soul its guidance. He has decreed this against them because He, glorified is He, knew that they were of the wretched, and that they were among those who choose misguidance over guidance.

The fā' (so) in His words, ﴿So taste [the punishment] for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾, marks the order of the command to taste following what came before it. The bā' (for) in ﴿for having forgotten﴾ indicates causation, and it implies that their punishment is not merely due to the preceding decree, but to that and this together.

Scholars differed about the forgetting mentioned here. Some said it is genuine forgetting, the kind by which remembrance departs. Others said it is abandonment. According to the first view, the meaning is that they did not work for that Day, so they were like those who forget it and do not remember it. According to the second, a noun must be supplied before ﴿meeting﴾: "taste the punishment of the meeting of this your Day because of your abandonment of what you were commanded." Al-Mubarrad preferred the second view and recited:

*As if it were a skewer of a drinker, one who forgot it at the moment of its drawing out (?)* [He made the poem's point that forgetting means abandoning.]

That is, they abandoned it. Al-Dahhak and Yahya ibn Salam also said that forgetting here means abandoning. Yahya ibn Salam said: The meaning is: For having abandoned belief in the Resurrection on this Day, We abandon you from good. Al-Suddi said the same. Mujahid said: We abandon you in the punishment.

Muqatil said: When they enter the Fire, the guardians will say to them, "Taste the punishment for having forgotten." Here the word "taste" is used metaphorically for experiencing. Tufayl said:

*So taste as we tasted on the day of the ambush,*
*From the rage in our livers and the reproach.*

His words: ﴿And taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do﴾ are a repetition for emphasis. That is: taste the lasting punishment that never ends, for what you used to do in the world of disbelief and sins.

Al-Razi said in his Tafsir (exegesis): the demonstrative in His words, ﴿for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾, may have three possible referents: it may refer to the meeting, to the Day, or to the punishment.

The clause ﴿Only those believe in Our signs﴾ is a new sentence that explains who deserves guidance to belief and who does not. The meaning is: only those who affirm Our signs and benefit from them are ﴿those who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration﴾, and not others who are reminded of them, that is, admonished by them, but do not remember or believe in them. The phrase ﴿fall down in prostration﴾ means fall on their faces, prostrating, glorifying Allah's signs and fearing His might and punishment. ﴿And glorify their Lord with praise﴾, that is, they declare Him free of all that is unbefitting Him, while joined with praise for His blessings, the greatest and most complete of which is guidance to belief. The meaning is that they say in their prostration: "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," or "Glory be to my Lord the Most High and praise be to Him."

Sufyan said: The meaning is "pray out of praise for your Lord." The clause ﴿and they are not arrogant﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while they are humbly submissive to Allah, abasing themselves to Him, and not arrogant toward Him.

**﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾**, that is, they rise and lift themselves up. It is said: *jafā al-shay' 'an al-shay'* and *tajāfā 'anhu* when a thing does not cling to another and is set aside from it. ﴿Beds﴾ is the plural of *maḍja'* (bed), the place where one lies down. Al-Zajjaj and al-Rummani said: *tajāfī* and *tajaffī* are toward the upward direction, and likewise in pardoning the one who errs in abuse or the like. ﴿Sides﴾ is the plural of *janb*. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: their sides are forsaking their beds. These are those who pray at night (*mutahajjidūn*), who rise from their bedding for prayer. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ata', and the majority. The prayer intended is the voluntary night prayer (*tanafful*, supererogatory worship) without specification.

Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: it is voluntary prayer between Maghrib and 'Isha'. It has also been said: it is the 'Isha' prayer alone, a report from al-Hasan and 'Ata'. Al-Dahhak said: it is the 'Isha' and Fajr prayers in congregation. It has also been said: they are those who rise for the remembrance of Allah, whether in prayer or otherwise.

**﴿They call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾.** This clause is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, relating to the pronoun in ﴿their sides﴾. So it is a circumstantial clause following another circumstantial clause. It is also possible that the first clause is a new sentence explaining one kind of their acts of obedience. The meaning is: their sides forsake their beds while they call upon their Lord, fearing His punishment and hoping for His mercy.

**﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾**, that is, from what We have provided them, or from their provision. This is the obligatory charity. It has also been said: it is voluntary charity. The better view is to take it in general. The accusative of *khawfan wa-ṭam'an* (in fear and hope) is causative (as a reason). It is also permissible for both to be verbal nouns in the accusative governed by an omitted verb.

**﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾.** The indefinite noun in the context of negation conveys generality. That is, no soul among souls, whichever soul it may be, knows what Allah, glorified is He, has hidden for those previously mentioned, of what will gladden their eyes. Al-Jumhur read *qurrati* in the singular. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah and Abu al-Darda' read *min qurrāt* in the plural. Hamzah read *mā ukhfiya* with a sukun on the yā', as an imperfect verb attributed to Allah, glorified is He. The rest read it with a fatḥah, as a passive past verb.

Ibn Mas'ud read *mā nukhfī* with a ḍammah on the nūn. Al-A'mash read *yukhfī* with a ḍammah on the yā' of the imperfect.

Al-Zajjaj said regarding the reading of Hamzah: the meaning is: some of what Allah has hidden for them. This is also the reading of Muhammad ibn Ka'b. The *mā* is in the accusative position.

Then, glorified is He, explained that this is because of their righteous deeds, saying: **﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾**, that is, for the sake of recompense for what they used to do in the world, or they are rewarded with that.

**﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiant?﴾** The interrogative is for denial, meaning: the believer is not like the defiant, for the difference between them has become clear. This is why He says, **﴿They are not equal﴾**. The plural form here is a further variation in expression of what the denial, conveyed by the interrogative, has conveyed. Al-Zajjaj said: He made two into a group when He said ﴿they are not equal﴾, because of the meaning of *min* (from, among). It is also said that it is because two is the least plural. The cause of its revelation will be explained at the end of the discussion.

Then, glorified is He, explained the outcome of the two groups, beginning with the believers, saying: **﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the gardens of refuge as a lodging﴾**. Al-Jumhur read *jannāt* in the plural. Talhah ibn Musarrif read *jannatu al-ma'wā* in the singular. *Al-ma'wā* is that to which they resort, and He attributed the gardens to it because it is the true refuge. It has also been said that *al-ma'wā* is one of the gardens, and this matter has been discussed earlier. The meaning of *nuzulan* (as a lodging/hospitality) is that they are prepared for them when they arrive. Originally it means what is prepared for the guest of food and drink, as we explained in Ali 'Imran. Its accusative is as a circumstantial clause.

Abu Haywah read *nuzlan* with a sukun on the zāy. The bā' in **﴿for what they used to do﴾** indicates causation, meaning: because of what they used to do, or because of their deeds.

Then He mentioned the other group, saying: **﴿As for those who defied﴾**, that is, departed from obedience to Allah and rebelled against Him and His messengers, **﴿their refuge is the Fire﴾**, that is, their abode to which they will go and in which they will settle is the Fire. **﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾**, that is, whenever they wish to leave it, they will be sent back into it, compelled and forced. It has also been said: when the flame pushes them to its top, they will be returned to their places. **﴿And it will be said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny"﴾**. The one who says this to them is the guardians of Hell from among the angels, or it is Allah, mighty and majestic. In this saying to them, while they are in the Fire, there is a degree of vexation to them that is not hidden.

**﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment﴾**, which is the punishment of the world.
